From Latin baptista, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin baptistērium, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστήριον (baptistḗrion).

From Old Galician-Portuguese bautizar, batiçar, a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptīzāre (“to baptise”), from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to immerse, plunge, baptise”).
Borrowed from New Latin Batrachia.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese baço, from Vulgar Latin *hepatium, from Ancient Greek ἡπάτιον (hēpátion), from ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”). Compare Spanish bazo. Related to hepático.

parole.significato: bay (body of water mostly surrounded by land)
parole.testo: From Late Latin baia, possibly from Iberian badia.
Learned borrowing from Latin bdellium.

parole.significato: to beatify (take step in declaring a person a saint)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin beātificāre (“to bless”). By surface analysis, beato + -ificar.

parole.significato: someone who has been beatified by the Catholic Church
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin beātus.
From beber + -dor, or from Latin bibitōrem.

From Old Galician-Portuguese beber, bever (“to drink”), from Latin bibere (“to drink”), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti. Cognate with Galician beber and Spanish beber, Catalan and Occitan beure, French boire, Italian bere and Romanian bea.
Possibly from Latin via + -eco, cf. Italian vico.
From Old Galician-Portuguese beijar, from Latin bāsiāre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese beijo, from Vulgar Latin *baisu(m), from Latin bāsium, from Proto-Indo-European *bu.

parole.significato: purslane (a plant of the family Portulacaceae, especially Portulaca oleracea)
parole.testo: Older verdoega, from Latin portulāca, possibly via Mozarabic [Term?]. Doublet of portulaca.
From Latin belga.
Learned borrowing from Latin bellicōsus.
Borrowed from Latin belligerantem.

parole.significato: to pinch (to squeeze a small amount of skin)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *vellicicāre, from vellicāre, most likely ultimately from vellus, the wool shorn from a sheep, fleece, or pelt.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bel, from Latin bellus, from Proto-Indo-European *dw-ene-, adverbial form of *deu- (“to do, perform, revere, show favor”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ben, from Latin bene (“well”).

parole.significato: welcome (whose arrival is a cause of joy)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bem vindo, from Vulgar Latin *bene venītus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, bem (“well”)
Semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin benedictus (“blessed”), perfect passive participle of Latin benedīcō (“to speak well of”). Doublet of bento, Bento, and Benedito.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin benedīcere. By surface analysis, bem + dizer. Doublet of benzer.

parole.significato: blessing (divine or supernatural aid or reward)
parole.testo: From bendizer + -ção, corresponding to Latin benedictiōnem (probably a semi-learned adaptation; compare the inherited doublet bênção).

parole.significato: Benedictine (of or pertaining to the Order of Saint Benedict)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Benedictīnus. By surface analysis, Benedito + -ino.
Borrowed from Latin beneficiārius (“enjoying a favor, granted a privilege”) from beneficium (“benefit”).
Borrowed from Latin beneficentia.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese beneficio, borrowed from Latin beneficium.

parole.significato: contributor (a benefactor; someone who gives to charity or some cause)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bene meritus.
From Late Latin beneplacitum. Cognate with Spanish beneplácito and Italian beneplacito.

parole.significato: budget that a curate obtains from ceremonies such as baptisms, weddings and burials
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bene esse (literally “being well, to be well”).
Borrowed from Latin benevolentem.
Learned borrowing from Latin benevolentia.

From Late Latin benefactōrem (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin benefaciō (“benefit someone”), from bene (“good”) + faciō (“do, make”). By surface analysis, bem + feitor. Compare Spanish bienhechor.
Learned borrowing from Latin benignus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese beento, bẽeyto, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin benedictus, perfect passive participle of Latin benedīcō (“to speak well (of)”). Doublet of bendito, a semi-learned borrowing, and Benedito.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bẽeizer, from Latin benedīcere. Doublet of bendizer. Compare Galician beicer.

parole.significato: beneficial (helpful or good to something or someone)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin beneficus.
Learned borrowing from Latin benevolus (“well-willing”).
Learned borrowing from Latin bēryllus, borrowed from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos), borrowed from Prakrit वेरुलिअ (vērulia), from Proto-Dravidian *weḷ-ūr (name of a city) + Prakrit -इय (-iya).

parole.significato: to yell loudly or angrily, to scream
parole.testo: Either imitative or inherited from Vulgar Latin *verrāre, from verrēs (“boar”). Compare Spanish berrear and Romanian zbiera.

From Old Galician-Portuguese verça (likely via Galician verza or a northern pronunciation), from Vulgar Latin *virdia, from Latin viridia, neuter plural of viridis. Compare Spanish berza, Italian verza, Romanian varză.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese besta, probably borrowed from Latin bēstia (“beast”). Doublet of bicha.

parole.significato: crossbow (weapon consisting of a bow mounted on a stock)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese baesta (“crossbow”), from Latin bālista, from Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra). Doublet of balista.
From Old Galician-Portuguese baesteiro, from Latin bālistārius, corresponding to besta (“crossbow”) + -eiro.
Borrowed from Late Latin bēstiālis, from Latin bēstia (“beast”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bēstiārium, from Latin bēstia.
Borrowed from Latin beta, from Ancient Greek βῆτα (bêta). The slang sense is a semantic loan from English beta.

From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca. Presumably came via a northern dialect or Galician on account of the /b-/. Compare Galician vexiga, Spanish vejiga. Doublet of vesico-, a borrowing from Latin.
Borrowed from Latin bis.
Borrowed from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “library”).

From Vulgar Latin bīstia, variant of Latin bēstia. Doublet of besta. Sense of "homosexual" possibly influenced by the sense of "prostitute" or by English bitch (also related to the possible origin in Portuguese).
From Vulgar Latin *bīstius, a masculine form of bīstia, from Latin bēstia (“beast”). Doublet of besta.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bico, from Latin beccus, from Gaulish *beccos (“chicken beak, small”), from Proto-Celtic *bekkos (“hook”). Possibly influenced by picar. Compare Spanish pico.
Learned borrowing from Latin bicolōrem.
Learned borrowing from Latin biennālis.
Borrowed from Latin biga.

parole.significato: bigatus (Roman coin bearing the figure of a bigae)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bīgātus.

From Vulgar Latin *bicŏrnĭa (“anvil”), from Latin bicornis (“two-horned”), from bi- (“two”) + cornī (“horns”), nominalized in the feminine with -a. Cognate with Spanish bigornia, Galician bigorna, French bigorne, early modern Italian bicornia, Andalusian Arabic, Moroccan Arabic, and Algerian Arabic
Borrowed from Latin bilis.
Inherited from Latin balaneola, diminutive of balanus.

parole.significato: bobbin (in a sewing machine, the small spool that holds the lower thread)
parole.testo: From Latin pilūlus, diminutive of pila (“ball”), from earlier birlo.
Learned borrowing from Latin bīmus, possible contraction of bis (“twice”) + hiems (“winter”).
Learned borrowing from Latin binōminis. By surface analysis, bi- + nominal. Piecewise doublet of binomial, binómino, and binómico.
Learned borrowing from Latin bīnārius. The sense of “torque” stems from how it is caused by forces in opposing directions.
Borrowed from French biologie, from German Biologie or New Latin biologia. By surface analysis, bio- + -logia. Piecewise doublet of zoologia.

parole.significato: bis (shows that something is to be repeated)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bis (“twice”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese biscoito, from Early Medieval Latin biscoctus (literally “twice-baked”). Compare Galician biscoito, Spanish bizcocho. Doublet of biscuit.
Learned borrowing from Latin bisōntem. Doublet of bisão.
From Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin epīscopātus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bispo, inherited from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos). Doublet of epíscopo. Compare Sicilian viscu.
Learned borrowing from Latin bisōn. Doublet of bisonte.
Borrowed from Late Latin habitācula, plural of habitāculum (“dwelling”).
Learned borrowing from Latin biennium.
Learned borrowing from Latin blanditia.

parole.significato: to blaspheme (to speak against God or religious doctrine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmāre. Doublet of lastimar, which was inherited.

parole.significato: blasphemous (lacking piety or respect for the sacred)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin blasphēmus, from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “profanity”).

parole.significato: an interesting story, joke or news
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese bõa, from Latin bona, feminine of bonus (“good”). Cognate with Galician boa and Spanish buena. See more at bom.
Borrowed from Latin boātus (“bellowing”). Compare Italian boato.

parole.significato: mouth (the opening of a creature through which food is ingested)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese boca, from Latin bucca, of Celtic origin.

parole.significato: yawn (open the mouth and take a deep breath)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *buccidiāre, formed from bucca (“mouth”), thus related to modern boca (“mouth”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese buxeta, from Vulgar Latin *buxita, from Late Latin buxis, borrowed from Ancient Greek πυξίς (puxís, “box”), from πῠ́ξος (pŭ́xos, “boxwood”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, feminine suffix). Doublet of boate and bússola. For the semantic development, compare English box (“vagina”).
Of uncertain and disputed origin. Perhaps from some derivation of Latin bucca (e.g. buccella).
From Old Galician-Portuguese voda (“wedding”), from Latin vōta (“vows”), plural of vōtum (“vow”). Cognate with English vow. Doublet of voto and bodo.

parole.significato: a small, cheap and possibly insalubrious tavern
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Latin apothēca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”). Doublet of adega, apoteca, botica, and butique.
Unknown. Possibly from Latin gōbius. Compare Italian gobione.

parole.significato: a donation of food traditionally given to the poor to mark an occasion
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vōtum (“vow”). Doublet of boda and voto.

parole.significato: common designation, extended to different species of teleost fish from the Sparidae family of seabreams and porgies.
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin bōca, from Ancient Greek βῶκα (bôka), accusative of βῶξ (bôx), a contracted form of βόαξ (bóax), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”).

From boi + -eiro, possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin, Late Latin bovārius or boārius (“cow herder”), from Latin bovārius, boārius (“of cattle”), from bōs.
Borrowed from Latin bōlētus, from Ancient Greek βωλίτης (bōlítēs).

parole.significato: bubble (a spherical volume of contained fluid)
parole.testo: From Latin bulla. Doublet of bola and bula.

parole.significato: mold (woolly or furry growth of tiny fungi)

From Old Galician-Portuguese bolssa, from Late Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa, “hide”). Doublet of bursa.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bõo, inherited from Latin bonus (“good”), from Old Latin duonos, earlier duenos, from Proto-Italic *dwenos. Doublet of bónus /bônus, a later borrowing. Compare Fala and Galician bo, Spanish bueno.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bondade, from Latin bonitātem.

parole.significato: doll (a toy in the form of a human)
parole.testo: Uncertain; see the Galician cognate. Maybe from Vulgar Latin *munnecca, *bunnecca, which also yielded Spanish muñeca, but meanings other than 'doll' (and derivates) don't match.
Perhaps from Latin bonus + aequus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese berbeleta of uncertain origin. Possible etymologies include: * Old Galician-Portuguese *belbeleta, from Vulgar Latin *belbellita, from bellus (“beautiful”). * Vulgar Latin *papilitta, from Latin pāpiliō (“butterfly”). Cognate with Galician bolboreta.
Unknown. Possibly from Latin laburnum, with the first syllable mistaken for a definite article.

parole.significato: stick, staff (stick that serves to support those who walk)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin burdōnem (“bastard, mule”).
Borrowed from Latin boreālis (“northern”), from Boreās, from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās, “personification of the north wind”).

parole.significato: tassel (ball-shaped bunch of plaited or otherwise entangled threads)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *burrula, diminutive of Late Latin burra. Compare Spanish borla.

parole.significato: sediment, grounds (collection of small particles, particularly dirt, that precipitates from a body of water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin burra.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *pustella, from Latin pustula. Compare Spanish postilla, Asturian postiella.

parole.significato: pharmacist; chemist (professional who dispenses pharmaceutical drugs)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin apothēcārius. By surface analysis, botica + -ário. Doublet of apotecário.

parole.significato: wineskin, water skin (container for liquids made out of animal hide)
parole.testo: Unknown. Perhaps from a derivative of Late Latin buttis, butta (“barrel, cask”), or otherwise related to bota (“boot”).
Created from Latin botulus + -ismo.
From Medieval Latin botanicus, from Ancient Greek βοτανικός (botanikós).
From Old Galician-Portuguese bouça, from Latin baltea, from balteus.

parole.significato: bovine (of or relating to the ox)
parole.testo: PIE word  *gʷṓws Learned borrowing from Late Latin bovīnus.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese braadar, from Vulgar Latin *balatrāre (“to shout, to shriek”), probably related to Latin balatrō (“charlatan”), probably from balō (“to baa”). Cognate with Galician bradar, Spanish baladrar, Catalan baladrejar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese branco, from Early Medieval Latin blancus, borrowed from Frankish *blank. Cognate with Galician branco, Spanish blanco. Doublet of Blanco and Bianca.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese brando, blando, from Latin blandus. Cognate with Galician brando, Spanish blando, Catalan bla, Italian blando and Romanian blând.

parole.significato: brachial (pertaining or belonging to the arm)

parole.significato: ember (a glowing piece of coal or wood)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese brasa, from Vulgar Latin *brasa, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Fala and Galician brasa.
Learned borrowing from New Latin brasīliānus.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to the city of Brasília, capital of Brazil
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin brasīliēnsis. By surface analysis, Brasília + -ense.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bravo, possibly from Vulgar Latin *bravus or *brabus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus.

parole.significato: Portuguese brace or fathom, a traditional unit of length about equal to 2.2 m
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese braça, from Latin brachia, variant of bracchium (“forearm, cubit”), from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn, “upper arm”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish braza, Catalan braça, and Italian braccia.
From braço + -al, or from Latin brachiālis, bracchiālis. Doublet of braquial. Compare Spanish brazal.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese braço, from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn, “arm”), from βραχύς (brakhús, “short”), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (“short, brief”). Compare Galician brazo, Spanish brazo, Catalan braç, Romanian braț, and Italian braccio.

Possibly inherited from Vulgar Latin *bragius, from Ancient Greek βράγος (brágos, “marsh, shallows”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to dig, bore”); compare Albanian bërrakë. Or, inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese brejo, from Proto-Celtic *bracum (“swamp”), from Proto-Indo-European
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brigna (“rocky terrain”).

Borrowed from Latin brevitātem. By surface analysis, breve (“brief”) + -idade.
From Vulgar Latin *vrincu, *vincru, *vinclu from Latin vinculum, from vinciō (“bind, fetter, tie”) + -culum. Doublet of vínculo and vinco.
Learned borrowing from Latin britannicus.

parole.significato: bronchopneumonia (bacterial infection of the lungs, characteristically showing numerous small foci of infection)
parole.testo: From bronco- + pneumonia, itself from Medieval Latin pneumonia, from Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía), from πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -ία (-ía).
From Vulgar Latin *bucculārius (“bossed”), from Latin buccula (“boss”), diminutive of bucca (“cheeck”), .
Borrowed from Late Latin brūchus.

parole.significato: mist (water or other liquid finely suspended in air)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese bruma, from Latin brūma.
Borrowed from Latin brūtālis.

parole.significato: raw, in the rough (in a natural state; unrefined)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bruto, a learned borrowing from Latin brūtus.

parole.significato: bract (leaf associated with a flower or cone)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bractea.
From Latin branchia.

parole.significato: bronchus (either or two branches of the trachea)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin bronchus, from Ancient Greek βρόγχος (brónkhos, “trachea, throat”).

Unknown. Traditionally held to be an irregular derivative of Latin mūsculus (“muscle”), perhaps originally referring to the back of the leg. PIE word  *gʷṓws Learned borrowing from Latin būcolicus, from Ancient Greek βουκολικός (boukolikós), from βουκόλος (boukólos, “drover, oxherd”), from βοῦς (boûs, “cow, ox”).
Borrowed from Latin būglōssa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bulla (“seal, sealed document; bull”), from Latin bulla (“bubble, rounded object”). Doublet of bola and bolha.

parole.significato: bulb (object that is spherical at one end and tapering at the other)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bulbus (“bulb, onion”), from Ancient Greek βολβός (bolbós, “plant with round swelling on underground stem”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese bulir /bolir, from Latin bullīre (“to bubble, to boil”), from bulla (“bubble”).
Learned borrowing from Latin bullītiō.
From Latin *budinum, from buda or budae.

parole.significato: pit; hole (hollow spot in a surface)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Old Galician-Portuguese furaco, through Vulgar Latin *foraculum from Latin forāmen (“aperture, opening”). Compare Galician buraco, furaco, furado, Asturian furacu, buracu, Ladino burako, Leonese buraco, Spanish buraco; compare also, just for the card games, Italian burraco a

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese burgo, from Late Latin burgus, from Vulgar Latin *burgus, borrowed from Frankish *burg (“fortified city”), from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“fortified city”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“high”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese burges, from Medieval Latin burgēnsis, from Latin burgus + -ēnsis. Equivalent to burgo + -ês and piecewise doublet of burguense. Compare Galician and Spanish burgués, Catalan burgès, French bourgeois and Italian borghese.
From Latin burricus. By surface analysis, burro + -ico.
Back-formation from burrico (“small donkey”), from Latin burricus (“small horse”), from burrus (“red-brown”), from Ancient Greek πυρρός (purrhós, “flame colored”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: bursa (sac where muscle slides across bone)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa). Doublet of bolsa.

parole.significato: pork sausage, typical of Trás-os-Montes, made with the animal's stomach and stuffed with backbone meat, bones and carti…
parole.testo: From Latin botellus. Cognate with Galician botelo, Asturian botiellu and Spanish botillo.

parole.significato: box (any of various evergreen shrubs or trees)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese buxo, from Latin buxus, from Ancient Greek πύξος (púxos). Cognate with Galician buxo, Spanish boj, Catalan boix, Occitan bois, French buis, Italian bosso, Romanian bucsău and English box.
From Latin būcina. Compare English buisine, Italian buccina. Doublet of bazuca.
From Latin bucceum, from bucca (“cheek”). Related to boca.

parole.significato: crosier (staff of a bishop or abbot)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin baculum, from Proto-Indo-European *bak-.
Inherited from Latin bacula, diminutive of bāca (“berry”).
From Latin balanus (“acorn”), from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”). Cognate with Catalan bàlan, French balane, Italian balano, Spanish bálano.

parole.significato: balsam (sweet-smelling oil or resin derived from some plants)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon).

From Old Galician-Portuguese barbaro, from Latin barbarus (“foreign, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, strange”), of onomatopoeic origin, mimicking the sound of foreign languages. Doublet of berbere and, possibly, of bravo /brabo.
Borrowed from New Latin Bavarus.
Learned borrowing from Latin bellicus.

parole.significato: birch (any of various trees of the genus Betula)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin betulla, diminutive of Gaulish betua, from Proto-Celtic *betwiyos, *betuyā (“birch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-. Compare Italian betulla, Spanish abedul, Catalan bedoll, French bouleau.

parole.significato: drunk; under the influence of alcohol

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bẽeiçon, from beençon (which yielded benção), from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin benedictiōnem (“blessing; benediction”), from benedictus, from Latin benedīcō. Borrowed from Latin biblicus (“biblical”). By surface analysis, Bíblia (“Bible”) + -ico.
Learned borrowing from Latin bifidus.
Borrowed from Latin bilis.

parole.significato: bipedal (of animals moving with two limbs)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bipedem.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin būfalus, from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos, “antelope, wild ox”).
From Medieval Latin Bulgarus, from Ottoman Turkish بولغار (bulgar). Doublet of bugre.

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin capitellum. Doublet of coudel, capitel, caudilho, capitelo, and cadete.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabelo (“hair”).

parole.significato: hairy, long-haired (having a lot of hair)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabeludo, from Vulgar Latin *capillūtus. By surface analysis, cabelo (“hair”) + -udo. Compare Spanish cabelludo, Italian capelluto and French chevelu.

parole.significato: to fit (no matter if space or volume is left)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese caber, from Latin capere (“to take in, contain”), from Proto-Italic *kapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyéti, from the root *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Compare Galician caber, Spanish caber, Italian capire (“to understand”) and Romanian încăpea.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cabeça, from Vulgar Latin capitia, from the neuter plural (reanalyzed as a feminine singular) of Latin capitium, from caput.

parole.significato: coat hanger (device, in the shape of shoulders, used to hang up coats, shirts, etc.)
parole.testo: Uncertain origin. parole.significato: chapter (a council or community of canons)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese cabidoo, from Ecclesiastical Latin capitulum (“ecclesiastical council or body”). Doublet of capítulo.

parole.significato: cape (piece of land extending beyond the coast)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabo (“besides; nearby”), from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-. Doublet of caput, chefe, and chef.
From Old Galician-Portuguese caboo, from Late Latin capulum (“rope; halter”), from Latin capiō (“to seize”). Doublet of cacho.

parole.significato: shard; piece (broken piece of ceramic or glass)

parole.significato: cacophony (a mix of discordant sounds, potentially creating ambiguities)

parole.significato: prison (place of long-term confinement for those convicted of serious crimes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cadea, from Latin catēna, from Proto-Italic *katesnā. Compare Galician cadea, Spanish cadena, and English chain. Doublet of the direct borrowing catena.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cadeira, from Vulgar Latin *cathēgra, variant of Latin cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “above”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “chair”). Doublet of cátedra, a borrowing.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cadela, from Latin catella (“female pup, young bitch”). Compare Galician cadela, Romanian cățea and Aromanian cãtsauã, cãtsau.

parole.significato: notebook (book in which notes or memoranda are written)

parole.significato: to fall; to fall down; to drop

Inherited from Latin dente canario (“canine tooth”).

From Vulgar Latin *callāre, from Latin chalāre, from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō).

parole.significato: heating (the act of making something hot)

From Latin callum (“callus”), from Proto-Indo-European *kal (“hard”).

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin calumniōsus. By surface analysis, calúnia + -oso.

Learned borrowing from Latin calvāria (“skull”). Doublet of caveira.

parole.significato: calvary (representation of the crucifixion of Jesus Christ)

Borrowed from Latin calvities. By surface analysis, calvo + -ície.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese calça, from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).

parole.significato: a cobbled street for pedestrian usage
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin calciāta (“paved road”), feminine of calciātus (“paved with limestone”), from Latin calcō (“trample”), from Latin calx (“limestone”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish calzada and French chaussée.

parole.significato: chamberlain (officer in charge of managing the household of a sovereign)

parole.significato: to walk (travel a distance by walking)

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caminho, from Late Latin cammīnus (“way”), from Gaulish. Compare Galician camiño.

parole.significato: campestral (relating to open fields or uncultivated land)

parole.significato: candela (unit of measurement of luminous intensity)

parole.significato: chaos (the unordered state of matter in classical accounts of cosmogony)

From Old Galician-Portuguese deçimo, borrowed from Latin decimus. Compare the inherited doublet dízimo.
Borrowed from Latin decuplus (“tenfold”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Daedalus, from Ancient Greek Δαίδαλος (Daídalos), named after the inventor of the maze in Greek mythology.

parole.significato: deficit, shortage (Deficiency in amount or quality)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin deficit.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin dēficit.
Inherited from Late Latin dē ex.
Learned borrowing from Latin digitus. Doublet of dedo, which was inherited.
From Late Latin diptycha, plural, from Ancient Greek, neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι (di) + -πτυχος (-ptukhos) (akin to Greek πτυχή (ptychí, “fold, layer”)).
Borrowed from Latin disparem.

parole.significato: debt (action, state of mind, or object one has an obligation to perform for another, adopt toward another, or give to a…
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese divida, devida, deveda, from Latin dēbita, plural of dēbitum, from dēbitus (“owed”), from dēbeō (“to owe”), from dē + habeō (“to have”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, to take”). Doublet of débito.
Inherited from Latin decimus. Doublet of décimo.

parole.significato: pity (feeling of sympathy at the misfortune or suffering of someone or something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese doo, from Late Latin dolus, from Latin dolor (“pain”). Compare Spanish duelo.
Learned borrowing from Latin docilis.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ducea, from a Vulgar Latin *duocina or ducēna, both ultimately from Latin duodecim (“twelve”).

parole.significato: and (connects two clauses indicating that the events occurred together, one after the other or without any special impl…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese e, from Latin et.
Learned borrowing from Latin eborēnsis.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēbullītiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin eburneus.
Borrowed from Latin ecclēsiālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós), from ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía).
Borrowed from Latin eclīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “eclipse”).
Borrowed from New Latin eclampsia, from Ancient Greek ἔκλᾰμψῐς (éklămpsĭs, “sudden development, violent onset”, literally “brightness”).

parole.significato: ecclesia (the public legislative assembly of Athens)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ecclēsia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía), from ἔκκλητος (ékklētos) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). Doublet of igreja, which was inherited.

parole.significato: echo (a reflected sound that is heard again by its initial observer)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin echō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂gʰ-.
Borrowed from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”).
Learned borrowing from Latin oeconomicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομικός (oikonomikós).

parole.significato: ecumenical (pertaining to the Christian Church worldwide)
parole.testo: From Late Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós).

parole.significato: eczema (acute or chronic inflammation of the skin)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin eczema, from Ancient Greek ἔκζεμα (ékzema).
Learned borrowing from Latin equuleus.

parole.significato: oedema (excessive accumulation of serum in tissue)
parole.testo: From New Latin edema, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “to swell”).
Learned borrowing from Latin aedificantis. By surface analysis, edificar + -ante.
Learned borrowing from Latin aedificāre (“to build, to erect, to establish; to create, to frame”).
Learned borrowing from Latin aedificātiōnem. By surface analysis, edificar + -ção.
Borrowed from Latin aedificium.
Learned borrowing from Latin aedīlis.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ēdictum. Doublet of édito.
Borrowed from Latin ēditor.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēditiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēducātōrem.
Learned borrowing from Latin educāre.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēducātiōnem. By surface analysis, educar + -ção.
Derived from Latin edulis.
Borrowed from Latin aedicula.

parole.significato: edible (that can be eaten without harm)
parole.testo: From Late Latin edibilis, from Latin edō (“to eat”).
From Latin effectus (“an effect, tendency, purpose”), from efficiō (“accomplish, complete, effect”).

parole.significato: event that is periodically commemorated on its anniversary
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ephēmeris.
Borrowed from Latin efferentem.
Borrowed from Latin effervēscentem.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin effectuāre.; compare French effectuer, Italian effettuare, Spanish and Catalan efectuar. From Latin effectus, perfect passive participle of efficiō (“to effect, to execute, to complete, to accomplish”).
Borrowed from Latin efficāx.
Borrowed from Latin efficientem.
Learned borrowing from Latin efficientia.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese eficácia, from Latin efficācia.
Borrowed from Latin effluere.
Borrowed from Latin effluvium.
Borrowed from Latin effūsus.

parole.significato: effusion, pouring out of a liquid, gas etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin effūsiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin effigiēs.

parole.significato: Aegean (of or relating to the Aegean Sea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aegaeus, from Ancient Greek Αἰγαῖος (Aigaîos, “Aegean”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ego (“I”). Doublet of eu.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēgregius.

parole.significato: Egyptian (of, from or relating to Egypt)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese egípcio, a learned borrowing from Latin aegyptius, borrowed from Ancient Greek Αἰγύπτιος (Aigúptios).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese eira (“threshing floor”), from Latin ārea (“threshing floor, open space”). Cognate to Galician eira, Spanish and Catalan era, Occitan ièra, French aire, Italian aia and Romanian arie. Doublet of área, borrowed from the same Latin word.

parole.significato: row (line of objects, often regularly spaced)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin ictus (“blow”).
Unknown. Possibly from Latin labes (“fault, defect, collapse”).

parole.significato: axle, axletree (the pin or spindle on which a wheel revolves)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese eixe, from Latin axis (“axletree”) (with change of declension), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”). Compare Galician eixe, Spanish eje. Doublet of the borrowing áxis.
Borrowed from Latin ēiaculārī (“hurl, shoot out”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēiectāre. Compare the inherited doublet enjeitar.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ēiectiōnem.
From Latin ille. Akin to Catalan el and Spanish el. False cognate of Arabic ال (al-).

parole.significato: third-person feminine singular nominative pronoun she; it
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ela, from Latin illa, feminine of ille. Cognate with Galician ela and Spanish ella.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēlabōrāre.
Learned borrowing from Latin elaborātiōnem. By surface analysis, elaborar + -ção.

parole.significato: they (a group of people other than the speaker, entirely female)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ellas, from Latin illās, accusative feminine plural of ille.

parole.significato: third-person masculine singular nominative personal pronoun; he; it
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ele, from Latin ille (“that, he, she, it”).

parole.significato: elephant (any mammal of the order Proboscidea)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese elefante, elifante, borrowed from Latin elephantis (“elephant”), from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās, “elephant, ivory”). Doublet of olifante.
Learned borrowing from Latin elephantiasis, from Ancient Greek ἐλεφᾰντῐ́ᾱσῐς (elephăntĭ́āsĭs).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēlegantem.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ēligere (“to choose, to elect”), from ex (“out of, from”) + legō (“choose, select, appoint”).
From Latin elegīa, from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεία (elegeía).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēlegantia (“elegance”), from ēligere (“to choose”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ēlēctus.
Borrowed from Latin ēlēctor. By surface analysis, eleger + -dor.

parole.significato: electress, wife of an Elector of the Holy Roman Empire
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ēlēctrīcem. Compare Spanish electriz, Catalan electriu, French électrice and Italian elettrice.
From Old Galician-Portuguese eleiçon, eiliçon, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin ēlēctiōnem.

parole.significato: element (one of the simplest or essential parts or principles of which anything consists, or upon which the constitutio…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin elementum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos). Compare Italian and Spanish elenco.

parole.significato: masculine third-person plural nominative personal pronoun; they
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese elos, from Latin illōs, influenced by the singular form.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēlēctīvus.
Learned borrowing from New Latin ēlectricitātem. By surface analysis, elétrico + -idade.

parole.significato: elevated; raised; high (at a great distance from the ground)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēlevātus, perfect passive participle of ēlevō (“to raise”).

parole.significato: to raise; to lift (to bring or take upwards)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ēlevāre (“to raise”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēlevātiōnem. By surface analysis, elevar + -ção.
Borrowed from Latin ēlīdere.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēlīmināre (“to carry out of doors; to eliminate”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese *ãelo, from Latin ānellus, diminutive of anus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₂no- (“ring”). See also the doublet anel, borrowed from Occitan.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēlogium (“inscription on a tombstone”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεῖον (elegeîon, “elegiac poem or inscription”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēloquentem.

parole.significato: eloquence (artistry and persuasiveness in speech or writing)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ēloquentia (“eloquence”).
Borrowed from Latin ēlūcidāre.
Borrowed from Latin ēlūcubrāre.

parole.significato: to elude, evade (largely substituted with iludir)
parole.testo: From Latin ēlūdere (“evade, elude”), from ē (“out of”), short form of ex, + lūdō (“play; trick”), with change in conjugation.
Learned borrowing from Latin aelūrus (“cat”) from Ancient Greek αἴλουρος (aílouros, “cat”).
From Latin ēlūsio.

From New Latin elasticus (“elastic”), from Ancient Greek as if *ἐλαστής (*elastḗs) for ἐλατής (elatḗs), equivalent to ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “a driver, hurler”), from ἐλαύνειν (elaúnein, “to drive, set in motion, push, strike, beat out”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin ēlectricus.

parole.significato: elliptical (in shape reminding of an ellipse, oval)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ellīpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós, “defective”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese en, from Latin in (“in”), from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”). Doublet of in.

parole.significato: to become leaner; to lose body weight
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enmagrecer, from Late Latin ēmacrēscere, from Latin macer (“lean”), from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. By surface analysis, e- + magro + -ecer.
Borrowed from Latin ēmānāre.
Borrowed from Latin ēmancipāre.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēmancipātiōnem. By surface analysis, emancipar + -ção.
Borrowed from Latin emasculāre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese envayr, from Vulgar Latin *invādīre, from Latin invādere (“to invade, to enter”).

parole.significato: to rock (move gently back and forth)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibilities include: * From abalar. * From Late Latin ballāre (“to play, dance”), prefixed with em-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbarricāre, from Latin in- + Vulgar Latin *barra. By surface analysis, embargo + -ar.
Inherited from Latin imbibere.
From Latin emblēma, from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma, “insertion”).

parole.significato: to ambush (to lie in wait for, or to attack)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin imboscāre, from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, thicket”).
Compare Spanish, Galician, and Catalan embriagar. Possibly from Vulgar Latin embriacāre, from Late Latin ēbriācus, from Latin ēbrius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin embryon, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, to swell”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese envurullar, envorullar, from Vulgar Latin *involūcrāre, from Latin involūcrum. By surface analysis, embrulho (“wrap”) + -ar.
From Late Latin imbūtum, from trāiectōrium imbutum, perhaps through Occitan. Cognate with Galician embude, Asturian embudu and Spanish embudo.
Uncertain. Perhaps inherited from Latin impositum according to 1914’s DRAE, of unknown origin according to recent editions.
From Old Galician-Portuguese emendar, enmendar, borrowed from Latin ēmendāre. Compare Spanish enmendar.
Borrowed from Latin ēmergentem.
Borrowed from Latin ēmergere.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ēmergentia, from Latin ēmergentem. By surface analysis, emergir + -ência.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēmigrantem. By surface analysis, emigrar + -ante.
Borrowed from Latin ēmigrāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin ēmigrātiōnem, from Latin ēmigrō (“to emigrate”).
Borrowed from Latin ēminentem.

parole.significato: emission (something that is emitted, especially the exhaust from a car)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmissiōnem (“sending forth”), from ēmittō (“send out”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mittō (“send”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”).
Borrowed from Latin ēmittere.
Borrowed from Latin emolumentum.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese empeecer, from Vulgar Latin *impedīscere, inchoative of Latin impedīre. Compare Galician and Spanish empecer
Inherited from Late Latin *impignāre, from pignus (“pledge”). Compare Spanish empeñar and Italian impegnare.
From en- + obsolete pértiga (“stick, staff, measuring stick”) + -ar. Portuguese pértiga is a semi-learned borrowing from Latin pertica (“staff, measuring rod”).
From Early Medieval Latin impeiōrāre, from Latin peiōrem (“worse”). By surface analysis, em- + pior + -ar.
Inherited from Latin ampulla. Doublet of ampola and âmbula.

parole.significato: to make someone eager or excited
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin *empollicāre, from pollēre (“to be strong or powerful”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese emprender, from Vulgar Latin *imprehendere. The current form came from the older emprehender, modified in a learned manner from the popularly inherited, now obsolete, form emprender to more closely reflect the Latin etymon, as with compreender and comprender, r

parole.significato: to impregnate (to cause to become pregnant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin impraegnāre. By surface analysis, em- + prenha + -ar. Doublet of impregnar.
From earlier empréstido (possibly influenced by préstimo), ultimately from Latin praestitus.

parole.significato: to push (apply a force to an object so that it moves away)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *enpurrar (attested as the hapax derived term enpurron); further etymology is uncertain. Cognate with Galician empurrar and, according to Joan Coromines, Asturian emburriar. Coromines claims the word is unrelated to empuxar and ultimately connects it to Latin p

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese empuxar /enpuxar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Late Latin impulsāre, from in- + pulsāre, or a frequentative of impellere. Doublet of impulsar, a learned borrowing, and possibly of empurrar. Cognate with Galician empuxar, Spanish empujar.

parole.significato: empirical (pertaining to or based on experience)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin empiricus.
Borrowed from Latin emporium (“market”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπορεῖον (emporeîon), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “marketer”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πόρος (póros, “travel”).
Borrowed from Latin aemulārī.

parole.significato: emeritus (retired but retaining an honorific version of previous title)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmeritus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese en-, from Latin in-, prefixation of Latin in (“in, into”); compare em.
From Vulgar Latin *incalciāre, derived from Latin calx (“heel”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese encantar. By surface analysis, en- + cantar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese encantaçon, from Latin incantātiōnem.

parole.significato: to incarcerate (to lock away in prison)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin incarcerāre. By surface analysis, en- + cárcere + -ar.
From encardir (“to make grubby”), from cárdeo (“thistle coloured”), from cardo (“thistle”), from Latin carduus (“thistle”).

Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, past participle of incarnō (“to make or become incarnate; to make into flesh”), from in- + Latin carō (“flesh”). Compare archaic Spanish encarnado, Asturian encarnáu.
Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnāre, from Latin carō (“flesh”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese encarnaçon, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātiōnem. Cognate with Galician and Spanish encarnación, Catalan encarnació, French incarnation and Italian incarnazione.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre. By surface analysis, en- + carregar. Compare Spanish encargar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese encetar, from Latin inceptāre (“to begin”). Compare Galician and Catalan encetar, and Spanish encentar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese encher, from Latin implēre. Compare Galician encher.

parole.significato: encyclopedia (reference work consisting of a list of words or expressions, not always arranged in alphabetical order, i…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin encyclopaedia (“general education”), a univerbated form of Koine Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδείᾱ (enkúklios paideíā), from ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios) + παιδείᾱ (paideíā).
From Late Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese encoller, from en- (“in-”) + coller (“collect”), from Latin colligō (“to collect”), from con- + legō (“to bring together, to gather, to collect”), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-.
From en- + Old Galician-Portuguese comendar, from Latin commendāre. Compare comandar, a doublet borrowed from French.
From Old Galician-Portuguese encontrar, from Vulgar Latin *incontrāre, from Latin in + contrā. Compare Italian incontrare, Old French encontrer, Spanish encontrar.

Uncertain, with many competing theories: * From encrenca (“trouble”) + -ar (Michaelis makes a circular etymology); * From encrenque (“useless person”) + -ar; * From Latin intricāre, making it a doublet of intrigar and intricar.

parole.significato: to encrypt (conceal information by means of a code or cipher)
parole.testo: From English encrypt + -ar, from en- + crypt, from Latin crypta (“vault”), from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”), from κρύπτω (krúptō, “to conceal”), from Proto-Indo-European *krāu-.
From encruzilhar (“to cross”), from cruz (“cross”), from Old Galician-Portuguese cruz, from Latin crux (“cross”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”).
From Latin *incruciculāre.
Internationalism. Learned borrowing from New Latin encephalon, from Ancient Greek ἐγκέφαλος (enképhalos, “within the head”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).
From Vulgar Latin *indērēctiāre, ultimately from Latin dīrēctus. Compare Italian indirizzare, Catalan endreçar, French adresser, Spanish enderezar.
Deverbal from endereçar (“to address”), ultimately from Latin dīrēctus (“straight”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese ãedlo, from Vulgar Latin *anēthulum, diminutive of anēthum, from Ancient Greek ἄνηθον (ánēthon). Cognate with Spanish eneldo.
From Latin indūrēscere, from indūrō. By surface analysis, en- + duro (“hard”) + -ecer. Compare Spanish endurecer.
Inherited from Late Latin *entubus, from Latin intŭbus.

parole.significato: enema (injection of fluid into the rectum)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin enema, from Ancient Greek ἔνεμα (énema, “injection”), from ἐνίημι (eníēmi, “to send in, inject”).

Learned borrowing from Latin energīa (“energy”), from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia, “action, act, work”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom.
Learned borrowing from Latin energūmenus. Compare English energumen.
Borrowed from Latin ēnervāre.
Inherited from Latin īnfatuāre.

parole.significato: to swathe (to bind with bandages or rollers)
parole.testo: Probably from en- + faixa + -ar, or less likely a Vulgar Latin *īnfasciāre, from Late Latin fasciāre, from Latin fascia. Compare Spanish fajar, Italian fasciare, Romanian înfășa.

parole.significato: to become ill; to get sick
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese enfermar, from Latin īnfirmāre (“weaken, shake”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enfermidade, enfermedade, from Latin īnfirmitātem.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enfermo, from Latin īnfirmus (“sick, feeble”), from in- + firmus (“firm”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”).

parole.significato: to thread (to put thread through an orifice, especially a pinhole)
parole.testo: From en- + fio (“thread”) + -ar, from Old Galician-Portuguese fio, from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

parole.significato: after a long time; eventually; at last
parole.testo: From em (“in”) + fim (“the end”). From Latin in fine. Compare French enfin.

parole.significato: emphyteusis (long-term right to use a property on condition of taking care of it and paying taxes)
parole.testo: From Latin emphyteusis, from Ancient Greek ἐμφύτευσις (emphúteusis, “tenure of a type of leasehold”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese enganar, from Early Medieval Latin ingannāre (“to trick, to deceive”) (attested in a gloss), from Latin gannīre. Compare Spanish engañar, Italian ingannare.
From Old Galician-Portuguese engenho, from Latin ingenium.
Possibly a semi-learned borrowing from Latin ingeniōsus.
Perhaps from Latin *irrugāre. Compare Galician engruñar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese anguia, Latin anguīllam, presumably in a form *anguīlam, to account for the elision of the /l/. Cognate with Spanish anguila.
From Latin hinnuleum.
Borrowed from Latin aenigma (“riddle”), from Ancient Greek αἴνιγμα (aínigma, “dark saying, riddle”).
From Latin aenigmaticus.

parole.significato: to get or cause someone to get disgusted or nauseated
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese anojar~enojar, from Late Latin inodiāre. Doublet of anojar and enojar. Compare Galician anoxar.
From en- + lear, from Latin ligo
Borrowed from Latin ēnōrmis.
Borrowed from Latin ēnormitātem (“irregularity; enormity”), corresponding to enorme + -idade.
From Old Galician-Portuguese *eisaio, from Late Latin exagium, from Latin exigō.

parole.significato: cove (a small coastal inlet, especially one having high cliffs protecting vessels from prevailing winds)
parole.testo: From en- + seio (“curve, bend”) + -ada, from Old Galician-Portuguese sẽo, from Latin sinus (“curve, bend”). Compare Spanish ensenada.
Inherited from Latin īnsidiāre.

parole.significato: to teach (to pass on knowledge to)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ensinar, from Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (also found in Medieval Latin), from Latin signāre.
Deverbal from ensinar (“to teach”), from Old Galician-Portuguese ensinar, from Vulgar Latin īnsignō (“to engrave”), Latin signum (“mark”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: to deafen (to make deaf, permanently or temporarily)
parole.testo: From en- + surdo (“deaf”) + -ecer, or from Latin surdēscere, from surdus (“deaf”) + -ēscō. Compare Spanish ensordecer.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin entem.

parole.significato: stepchild (the child of one's spouse and his or her previous partner)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese entẽado, from Latin ante nātus (“born before”).
Borrowed from Late Latin entelechīa, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia).

parole.significato: to understand, to grasp, to comprehend
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese entender, from Latin intendere. Doublet of intender, a borrowing.
From en- + Latin tenebrēscere (“to darken, to become dark”) (a borrowing), from tenebrae (“darkness”).

parole.significato: to bury, to inter, to entomb
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese enterrar, from Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put into earth”), from Latin terra. By surface analysis, en- + terra + -ar.
Learned borrowing from Latin entheus, from Ancient Greek ἔνθεος (éntheos).

parole.significato: entity (something or somebody that exists as an individual unit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin entitātem.

parole.significato: enthymeme (syllogism in which a premise or conclusion is implied)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin enthȳmēma, from Ancient Greek ἐνθύμημα (enthúmēma).

parole.significato: bowel (an internal organ of the stomach)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese entranna, from Latin interānea, from the plural of Latin interāneum (“gut, intestine”), substantive of interāneus (“internal, inward”). Compare Spanish entraña, Catalan entranya, and French entrailles.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese entrar, intrar, from Latin intrāre.

parole.significato: among (denotes a mingling or intermixing with distinct or separable objects)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese entre, antre, from Latin inter (“between; among”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”).
Inherited from Latin inter-. Doublet of inter-.

parole.significato: to deliver (to transport something to a destination)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese entregar, probably a semi-learned term taken from Latin integrāre. Doublet of integrar and inteirar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intervidēre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese entroydo, from Latin introitus. Cognate with Galician entroido, Mirandese antruido and Asturian antroxu.

Borrowed from Late Latin enthūsiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós, “inspiration, enthusiasm”), from ἔνθεος (éntheos, “possessed by a god”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese enton, from Vulgar Latin *in tunc, from Latin in + tunc (“then”). Displaced collateral form entonce. Compare Spanish entonces.
Borrowed from Latin ēnumerāre.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēnumerātiōnem (“enumeration”). By surface analysis, enumerar + -ção.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēnūntiāre (“to reveal, to express”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese enviar, from Late Latin inviāre, from Latin via (“path, road”). Compare Spanish and Catalan enviar, French envoyer, Italian inviare.
From Vulgar Latin *involtus, from *involvitus or *involŭtus, for Latin involūtus. Doublet of involuto.
From Latin involvere (“to involve”), from in (“in, at, on”) + volvō (“to roll”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to turn, wind, round”).
From Vulgar Latin *asciāta, from Latin ascia. Compare Galician aixada, Spanish azada, and Catalan aixada.

parole.significato: to rinse (to remove soap from something using water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exaquāre with a change in prefix.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese eixame, from Latin exāmen. Doublet of exame, a learned borrowing. Cognate with Galician enxame, Spanish enjambre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese serga, from Latin sērica (with a later prefix en- added in Portuguese). Compare Galician xerga, Spanish jerga, French serge (whence Portuguese sarja).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin īnsertāre (“to insert”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese suffre (with the prefix en-), from Latin sulfur, sulphur, suphure, from Proto-Indo-European *swelplos, from the root *swel- (“to burn, smoulder”). Compare Galician xofre and Spanish azufre. Doublet of súlfur.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin exsūcāre, with a change of prefix. Compare Spanish enjugar.

From Old Galician-Portuguese enxoyto, from Latin exsūctus (with a change of prefix), past participle of exsūgō, from ex + sūgō. Compare Galician enxoito, Spanish enjuto, Catalan eixut, Italian asciutto.
From Late Latin asciola, from Latin ascia. Compare Galician aixola, Spanish azuela.
Borrowed from Latin ē̆ōus, from Ancient Greek ἠῷος (ēōîos), ἑῷος (heōîos, “of the east; of the morning”), derived from ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”). Compare English eoan, Italian eoo.
From Latin epicoenus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκοινος (epíkoinos), based on κοινός (koinós, “common”).

parole.significato: epicycle (a small circle whose centre is on the circumference of a larger circle)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin epicy̆clus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos). By surface analysis, epi- + ciclo.
Borrowed from Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”).
Borrowed from Latin epidermis (“epidermis”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís), from ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”).

parole.significato: epiglottis (cartilaginous organ in the throat of terrestrial vertebrates)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin epiglōttis. By surface analysis, epi- + glote.
Learned borrowing from Latin epilēpsia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψία (epilēpsía), from ἐπιλαμβάνω (epilambánō, “to seize”).
Learned borrowing from Latin epilēpticus. By surface analysis, epilepsia + -ico.
Borrowed from Late Latin episcopālis.

Latin epithalamium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”), neuter form of ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).
Borrowed from New Latin epithēlium.
From modern Latin epizeuxis, from Ancient Greek ἐπίζευξις (epízeuxis, “a fastening upon”), from ἐπιζευγνύναι (epizeugnúnai), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + ζευγνύναι (zeugnúnai, “to yoke”).

parole.significato: a bishop, especially during the early Christian church
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos). Doublet of bispo.
Borrowed from Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ).

Borrowed from Latin epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton), neuter form of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “added”), from ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi, “to add on”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, to place”).
Borrowed from Latin epitomē.
Borrowed from Latin aequātōrem (“equalizer”).

parole.significato: to level out; to make uniform
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aequalis (“equal”) + -izar. Possibly influenced by English equalize.
Learned borrowing from Latin aequātiōnem.
From Latin equester.

parole.significato: equidistant (occupying a position that is an equal distance between several points)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aequidistantem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aequilībrāre (“to weigh out, to apportion”), from Latin aequilībris (“of the same weight, in balance”).

parole.significato: equilateral (whose sides are of equal length)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aequilaterus.
Learned borrowing from Latin aequilībrium.
Learned borrowing from Latin equīnus, from equus (“horse”), from Old Latin equos (“horse”), from Proto-Italic *ekwos (“horse”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éḱwos (“horse”).
Learned borrowing from Latin echīnus, from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos).
Learned borrowing from New Latin echinoderma. By surface analysis, equino- + -dermo.
PIE word  *nókʷts From Latin aequinoctium (“equinox”), from aequus (“equal”) + nox (“night”) (ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”)) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).
From Latin aequiparāre, an alternative form of aequiperō (“to put on a level with, compare, liken”).
Learned borrowing from Latin equitātiōnem, from equitātus, from equitō (“to ride a horse”), from equus (“horse”).
Borrowed from Latin aequivalēre. Equivalent to equi- + valer.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aequivalentia.
From Late Latin aequivocāre. Cognate with English equivocate.
Borrowed from Latin aequanimis.
From Late Latin aequivocus (“equivocal, ambiguous”).

parole.significato: era (time period of indeterminate length, generally more than one year)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin aera.

parole.significato: synonym of erásmico (“of or pertaining to Erasmus of Rotterdam”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Erasmiānus, from Erasmus. By surface analysis, Erasmo + -iano.

parole.significato: Erasmus (an exchange student taking part in an Erasmus Programme)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin Erasmus. Doublet of Erasmo.

parole.significato: pre-reform spelling (used until 1943 in Brazil and 1990 in Portugal) of ereção; still used where the agreement hasn’t c…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ērectiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin erēmīta, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs).
Learned borrowing from Latin ērectus. Compare the inherited doublet hirto.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ērēctiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin ergō.

From Old Galician-Portuguese erger, from Vulgar Latin *ergere, from Latin ērigere. The modern verb has been rebuilt around the conjugation ergo (“I raise”), hence the other inflexions now all have /ɡ/ rather than the /ʒ/ one would expect from medieval forms like erger. Galician erguer and Spanish er
Learned borrowing from Latin ergastulum.

parole.significato: to set up; to construct; to build
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ērigere. Doublet of erguer, which was inherited.
From Scientific Latin erythema, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ermo, hermo, from Late Latin eremus, from Latin erēmus, from Ancient Greek ἔρημος (érēmos), with preservation of Greek accent over vowel length in Late Latin. Compare Aromanian ermu
From Latin ērōdō.
Learned borrowing from Latin ērōsio, from ērōdō.
Borrowed from Latin ērādīcāre (“uproot”).
Borrowed from Latin errantem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese errar, from Latin errāre (“to err”).

parole.significato: to err is human (everybody makes mistakes)
parole.testo: Calque of Latin errāre hūmānum est.
Borrowed from Latin errāta. Doublet of errada.
Learned borrowing from Latin errōneus.

parole.significato: caterpillar (the larval stage of a lepidopteran)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin eruca (“caterpillar, arugula”). Doublet of eruga, which was inherited (compare Galician eiruga).
Borrowed from Latin ērūctāre. Doublet of arrotar.
Borrowed from Latin ērudītus.
Inherited from Latin eruca. Compare Galician eiruga.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēruptiōnem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese erva, from Latin herba, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”). Cognate with Galician herba and Spanish hierba.
From Latin ervilia (“type of vetch”). Compare Spanish arveja and ervilla.
Borrowed from Latin aerārium (“treasury”).
Learned borrowing from Latin erōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐρωτῐκός (erōtĭkós).
Inherited from Latin ex- (“out of”). Doublet of ex-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese esbullar (compare Galician esbullar), from Latin spoliāre. Compare the borrowed doublet espoliar, and cf. also espojar.
Inherited from Latin scabellum, diminutive form of scamnum.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escaada, from Vulgar Latin *scālāta, from Latin scāla (“stair, staircase, ladder”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scāla. Doublet of escada (“ladder, stairs”).

parole.significato: of, from or relating to Santarém, Portugal
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin scalabitānus, from Latin Scalabis.
From Late Latin excaldāre, from Latin cal(i)dus (“hot”).
From Vulgar Latin *excalfāre, from Latin excal(e)facere.

parole.significato: common name for several teleost fish of the Cyprinidae family, of freshwater, very common in Portugal.
parole.testo: From Latin squalus (“large seafish”).
Borrowed from Latin scalpellum.

parole.significato: scale (keratin pieces covering the skin of certain animals)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese escama, from Latin squāma (“scale”).

parole.significato: to barter (to exchange goods or services without involving money)
parole.testo: An alteration of escambiar, from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre. By surface analysis, escambo + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre. By surface analysis, es- + cambiar.
From escama + -oso, or from Latin squāmōsus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, escândalo + -izar.

From Old Galician-Portuguese escano, from Latin scamnum, from Proto-Italic *skaβnom, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ-no-m, from *skabʰ- (“to hold up”). Cognate with Galician escano, Spanish escaño, Italian scanno, Sanskrit स्कम्भ (skambhá). Doublet of escanho.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escapar, from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin scaccum, from Arabic شَاه (šāh, “shah; king in chess”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin scarabaeus (“beetle”), from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”).

parole.significato: to mock; to make fun of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escarnir, from Late Latin *scarnīre, *scernīre, possibly through an Old French or Old Occitan intermediary.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escasso, from Vulgar Latin *excarsus, for Latin excerptus, from excerpō. Thus doublet of excerto.
Inherited from Latin excavāre.
Borrowed from New Latin sclera, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”).
From escoar (“to drain”) + -mento, from es- + coar (“to filter”), from Latin cōlāre (“to filter”).
Inherited from Latin *excōlāre. Compare Galician escoar, Spanish escolar, French écouler, Italian scolare, and Sicilian sculari.

parole.significato: school (institution dedicated to teaching and learning)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese escola, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “spare time, leisure”). The Portuguese form may indicate a semi-learned influence on the phonetic aspects of the word.
From Late Latin scholāris, from Latin schola.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escolher, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *excolligere, from Latin ex- + colligere (“to gather”). Compare Galician escoller, Spanish escoger, Catalan escollir.

parole.significato: scholastic (relating to scholasticism, medieval philosophical system)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin scholasticus, from Ancient Greek σχολᾰστῐκός (skholăstĭkós).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese asconder, from Latin abscondere. Doublet of absconder, a borrowing.

Semi-learned borrowing from Latin abscōnsus (“hidden”), perfect passive participle of abscondō. Cf. the doublets absconso (a later borrowing) and escuso (a popularly inherited form). Compare the related Spanish escusa, escuso, escusar, Galician escuso, escusar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escorpiõ, from Latin scorpiōnem (“scorpion”), from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos).

parole.significato: to slide (to move on a low friction surface)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escorregar, from Vulgar Latin *excurricāre.
Inherited from Latin excurrere.

parole.significato: Gael (member of an ethnic group of Ireland and western Scotland in Antiquity and the Middle Ages)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Scōtus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Latin scōpa (“broom”). False friend to Spanish escoba.
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Late Latin scōpāre (“to brush or sweep away”), from Latin scōpae (“broom”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”). Doublet of eslavo, esloveno, esclavão /eslavão, and tchau /chau.

From Old Galician-Portuguese escrever, escrivir, from Latin scrībere (“to write”), from Proto-Italic *skreiβō, from Proto-Indo-European *skreybʰ- (“to write”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish escribir, Catalan and Occitan escriure, French écrire, Italian scrivere, Romanian scrie and English shrive

parole.significato: scribe (someone employed to write and take notes)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scriba. Doublet of escrivão.

parole.significato: writing (written letters or symbols that express some meaning)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese escrita, from Latin scrīpta, feminine form of scrīptus (“written”), from scrībō (“to write”), from Proto-Indo-European *skreybʰ-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escrito, from Latin scrīptus. Doublet of script.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escriptor, from Latin scriptor, scriptōrem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escriptura, from Latin scrīptūra (“a writing, scripture”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scrīptōrium.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escrivan, from Vulgar Latin *scrībānem, from alteration of declension from Latin scrība (“writer, scribe”). Doublet of escriba, a borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Latin scrōtum.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin scrūpulōsus. By surface analysis, escrúpulo + -oso.
Learned borrowing from Latin scrōfula.

parole.significato: Portuguese scruple, escropulo a traditional unit of mass equivalent to about 1.2 g
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin scrūpulus. Doublet of escrúpulo. Cognate with Spanish escrúpulo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escudeiro, escudeyro, from Late Latin scūtārius, from Latin scūtum. By surface analysis, escudo + -eiro.

From Old Galician-Portuguese escudo (“shield”), from Latin scūtum (“shield”), from Proto-Indo-European *skei- (“to cut, split”), which is an extension of *sek- (“to cut”). The name of the currency comes from the heraldic shields on the coins.

parole.significato: to carve (shape a piece of material into an object)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sculpere.
Borrowed from Latin sculptor.

parole.significato: sculpture (work of art created by sculpting)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sculptūra.
Latin Aesculapius
Probably blend of Latin spūma and a Germanic skum, from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz. Compare Catalan escuma, French écume.
Inherited from Latin obscūritās. By surface analysis, escuro + -idade.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escuro, scuro, oscuro, from Latin obscūrus. Doublet of obscuro. Compare Sicilian scuru.
Borrowed from Latin scurra. Compare Spanish escurra.

parole.significato: to forgive; to pardon; to excuse
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese escusar, from Latin excūsāre.

parole.significato: to listen to; to hear (to perceive sound)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese escuitar, ascuitar, ascoitar, from Latin ascultāre. Compare Galician escoitar. Doublet of auscultar, a borrowing from Latin.
Learned borrowing from Latin scapula (“shoulder”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scandalum, from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon), from Proto-Indo-European *skand- (“to jump”).
Borrowed from Latin scoria, from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphēra, from Latin sphaera, borrowed from Ancient Greek σφαῖρᾰ (sphaîră, “ball, globe”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sphingem, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ (Sphínx).
From Old Galician-Portuguese esfolar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin *exfollāre. By surface analysis, es- (“ex-”) + fol (“hide, skin, bag”) + -ar.
From Latin exfoliare, from exfolio. Cognate with Galician esfollar, Spanish exfoliar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin exfrīgidāre, from Latin ex- (intensifying prefix) + Late Latin frīgidāre (“to make cold”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sphaericus. By surface analysis, esfera + -ico.
From Latin exiguus. Doublet of the borrowing exíguo.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Slavus, from Sclavus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more. Doublet of escravo, esloveno, esclavão /eslavão, and tchau /chau.
Inherited from Latin aestimare. Doublet of estimar, which displaced this word.
Learned borrowing from Latin smēgma.

parole.significato: to hone (to refine or master a skill)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exmerāre (“to purify”), from Latin ex merēre. Compare Spanish esmerar.

parole.significato: to break down, to detail (to explain carefully and in detail)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from es- + Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre, derived from Latin minūtus. Compare Galician esmiuzar.

parole.significato: alms (small amount of money or goods given to someone as charity)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese esmolla, esmolna, earlier elmosna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē).

From Vulgar Latin emorescĕre, frequentative of Latin ēmori, ēmorior (“to die (out)”), from Latin morior (“to die”), whence Portuguese morrer (“to die”); but note also Old English smorian (“to choke, suffocate”). Cognate to Galician and Spanish esmorecer.
From es- + palha (“straw”) + -ar, from Latin palea (“straw”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Spanish and Catalan espantar, Italian spaventare, French épouvanter.
From Medieval Latin sparadrapum, of obscure origin. Compare Spanish esparadrapo, Catalan esparadrap, French sparadrap, Italian sparadrappo, Sicilian sparatrappu.

parole.significato: to scatter, to strew, to spread
parole.testo: From Latin spargō (“scatter”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pregʰ- (“to scatter, to jerk”).
From Medieval Latin sparagus, asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).

parole.significato: sparse (whose elements are far from each other)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sparsus.
Borrowed from Latin Spartānus (“Spartan”). Analyzed as Esparta + -ano.
Borrowed from Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós).

parole.significato: to shatter, to break into pieces
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps ultimately from Latin patefaciō (“to throw open”).
Either from es- + pavor + -ar, or from a Vulgar Latin *expavorīre, from *pavorīre, from pavor. Compare Italian spaurire, Occitan espavordir; cf. also Romanian speria.

parole.significato: to space (to be separated to a distance)
parole.testo: From espaço (“space”) + -ar, from Latin spatium (“space”), from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- (“to stretch, to pull”).
Borrowed from Latin speciālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin speciālitātem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin specificāre. By surface analysis, específico + -ar or espécie + -ificar.
Borrowed from Latin speciōsus (“good-looking”).
Borrowed from Latin spectātōrem, from spectō (“to watch”), from speciō (“to look at”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ-.
Learned borrowing from Latin spectrum.
Learned borrowing from Latin speculātōrem. By surface analysis, especular + -dor.
Learned borrowing from Latin speculārī.
Borrowed from Late Latin speculātīvus, from Latin speculor. By surface analysis, especular + -tivo.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor. By surface analysis, especular + -ção. Compare Galician especulación.
Borrowed from Late Latin specificus, from speciēs (“kind”) + faciō (“make”).

parole.significato: mirror (smooth surface, usually made of glass with reflective material painted on the underside)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese espelho, from Vulgar Latin speclum, syncopated form of Latin speculum. Compare Galician espello and Spanish espejo. Doublet of espéculo.

parole.significato: spelt (a type of wheat, Triticum spelta or Triticum aestivum subsp. spelta)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spelta.
From Latin spēlunca, from Ancient Greek σπῆλυγξ (spêlunx), from earlier σπέος (spéos).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese asperança, from Latin spērāns, from spērō, from Old Latin *spēsō, from spēs (“hope”) + -ō (verbal suffix). By surface analysis, esperar + -ança. Compare Spanish esperanza, French espérance, Italian speranza.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese asperar, from Latin spērāre, from Old Latin *spēsō, from spēs (“hope”) + -ō (verbal suffix).
From Old Galician-Portuguese esperto, from Latin expertus, from Latin expergitus, from expergo. Doublet of experto and expert.
From Old Galician-Portuguese espesso, from Latin spissus, from Proto-Indo-European *spidtos.
Learned borrowing from Latin spectāculum (“show, spectacle”).

parole.significato: to spy (to act as a spy)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *spiāre, from Gothic or Frankish *spehōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese espiga, from Latin spīca (“spike”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp, sharp stick”). Cognate with Galician, Spanish, and Catalan espiga, Occitan espic, French épi, Italian spiga and Romanian spic.
From Old Galician-Portuguese espigar, from Latin spīcāre.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese espinha, from Latin spīna (“thorn”), from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp point”). Cognate with Galician espiña. The sense of "spine" or "thorn" was lost to espinho.

parole.significato: thorn (sharp protective spine of a plant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese espinho, from Latin spīnus (“thorn-bush”).
From espinho + -oso, possibly corresponding to Latin spīnōsus.
From Latin spira.
Borrowed from Latin spīrāre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin spīrituālis. By surface analysis, espírito + -ual.
Inherited from Latin expīrāre (“to exhale, to die”), alternative form of exspīrō. Doublet of expirar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese esplandor, esprandor, from Latin splendor.
Learned borrowing from New Latin splanchnicus, from Ancient Greek σπλαγχνικός (splankhnikós), from σπλάγχνα (splánkhna, “viscera”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).
