parole.significato: exsiccatum (dried specimen such as that in a herbarium)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exsiccāta.
Borrowed from Latin exsūdāre (“to sweat out”), from ex- with sūdāre (“to sweat”), from sūdōris (“of sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- or *sweyd-.
Borrowed from Latin exsurgere.

parole.significato: extemporaneous, inopportune (occurring or appearing at an inconvenient or inappropriate time)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin extemporāneus.
Borrowed from Latin extēnsus, perfect passive participle of extendō (“extend, stretch out”).
Learned borrowing from Latin extēnsiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin extenuāre.
Learned borrowing from Latin extenuātiōnem. By surface analysis, extenuar + -ção.
Borrowed from Latin exterior.
From Latin exterminātōrem. By surface analysis, exterminar + -dor.
Learned borrowing from Latin extermināre.
Borrowed from Latin exterminātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin exterminium.
Learned borrowing from Latin externus.
Learned borrowing from Latin extinguere.
Borrowed from Latin exstinctus or extinctus.
From Latin exstīnctor.

parole.significato: extinguishment (act of putting out a fire)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin extīnctiōnem, from extīnctus, perfect passive participle of extīnguō (“to extinguish”).
Borrowed from Latin exstirpāre (“uproot”).
Borrowed from Latin exstirpātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin extorquēre. Compare estorcer < V. Latin *extorcere.

parole.significato: extortion (the practice of extorting money or other property)
parole.testo: From Late Latin extortiō, from extorqueō.
Learned borrowing from Latin extrā-, from extrā (“outside, beyond”).
Learned borrowing from Latin extrahere, with change of conjugation.
Learned borrowing from Latin extrāōrdinārius. By surface analysis, extra- + ordinário.
Learned borrowing from Latin extractum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin extrāvagantem.
Learned borrowing from Latin extractiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin extrēmus.
Learned borrowing from Latin extro- + versio. Similar to English extraversion.
Learned borrowing from Latin extrūdere.
Borrowed from Latin exūberantem.
Borrowed from Latin exsultāre.

parole.significato: exultation (lively joy at success or victory)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exsultātiōnem. By surface analysis, exultar + -ção

parole.significato: to exhume (to take out of a place of burial)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin exhumāre, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).
From Latin exanimis.
Learned borrowing from Latin exsequiās.
Borrowed from Latin exercitus.
From Latin exitium.
Borrowed from Latin exiguus (“strict, exact, scanty, meager”), from exigō (“to drive out”). Doublet of esguio.
Borrowed from Latin exilium, exsilium. Displaced Old Portuguese eixillo.
Borrowed from Latin eximius.
Learned borrowing from Latin exōticus.

parole.significato: to manufacture, to fabricate (to make things, usually on a large scale, with tools and either physical labor or machine…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fabricāre.
Learned borrowing from Latin fābricātiōnem. By surface analysis, fabricar + -ção.
Learned borrowing from Latin fābulōsus.
Unknown. Possibly from Latin falx (“sickle”). Cognate with Galician faca.
Learned borrowing from Latin factiōsus. By surface analysis, facção + -oso.
From Old Galician-Portuguese façe, faz, from Latin faciēs. Doublet of fácies.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fascŭlō, from fax (“torch”). Compare Galician facho.
Borrowed from Latin faciālis.
Borrowed from Latin facilitātem.
Learned borrowing from Latin factum. Doublet of feito.
Learned borrowing from Latin factīcius. Doublet of feitiço, which was inherited, and fetiche, a reborrowing from French.
Learned borrowing from New Latin factotum.
Learned borrowing from Latin facultātem.
Borrowed from Latin facetia.
From Latin facinora, plural form of facinus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese fada, from Vulgar Latin *Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Galician, Catalan, and Occitan fada, Spanish hada, French fée and Italian fata.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin fatīgāre.
Inherited from Latin fātum (“destiny, fate”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese fagulla, from a Vulgar Latin root *facucla, from syncopation of *facucula, from Latin facula. Doublet of fácula, a borrowing, and of facha. Compare Sicilian faviḍḍa.
From Latin fagus (“beech”) and Ancient Greek πυρός (purós, “wheat”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese faia, from Latin fāgea, nominalization of [materia] fāgea (“beech wood”), derived from Latin fāgus (“beech tree”). Compare Galician faia, Asturian faya, Spanish haya, and Catalan faja.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fala, from Latin fābula (“discourse, narrative”). Doublet of fábula, a learned borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Latin phalangem (“phalanx”), from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “battle order, array”). Compare also the related palanca.

parole.significato: to speak; to talk (to say words out loud)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese falar, from Latin fābulārī (“chat, converse”). Doublet of fabular, which was borrowed from Latin. Compare Galician falar, Spanish hablar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese falcon, from Late Latin falcōnem, probably of Germanic origin.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese falescer, derived from falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere. Cognate with Galician falecer, Spanish fallecer.

From Latin phalaena, from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina, “moth; whale”). The semantic shift from "whale" to "moth" occurred in Hellenistic Greek, likely due to an analogy between the fluttering movement of a moth's wings and the fins or spout of a whale.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Classical Latin fallere, possibly from Proto-Italic *falsō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el-.
Learned borrowing from Latin faliscus.
From Latin phallus, from Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós)
From Old Galician-Portuguese falsidade, falssidade, from Late Latin falsitātem. By surface analysis, falso + -idade.

parole.significato: to falsify (to alter so as to be false)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin falsificāre (“to make false, to corrupt, to counterfeit, to falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”). By surface analysis, falso + -ificar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese falso, from Latin falsus (“deceived”), from fallō (“to deceive”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰwel- (“to lie, deceive”).

parole.significato: lack (the condition of not having, needing, or needing more of something)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese falta, from Vulgar Latin *fallita, feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō. Cognate to Catalan falta, English fault, Spanish falta and French faute.
Learned borrowing from Latin fallācia (“deception, deceit”).
From Latin fallentia, plural of fallēns, from fallō (“to deceive”). By surface analysis, falir + -ência.

parole.significato: fallible (capable of making mistakes or being wrong)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin fallibilis (“liable to err, also deceitful”), from Latin fallō (“to deceive, trick, cheat, disappoint”). By surface analysis, falir + -ível.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fama, from Latin fāma, from Proto-Indo-European *bheh₂-mā-, from *bheh₂- (“to speak”).
Borrowed from Latin fāmigerātus (“famed”).
Borrowed from Latin familiāris.

parole.significato: familiarity; acquaintance (state of being familiar with something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin familiāritātem.
From earlier famiinto, from Old Galician-Portuguese famĩento, from Vulgar Latin *faminentus, from Latin famēs (“hunger”). Cognate with Galician famento and Spanish hambriento.
Learned borrowing from Latin fāmōsus. By surface analysis, fama (“fame”) + -oso (“-ous”).
Learned borrowing from Latin famēlicus (“hungry, famished”). Doublet of famelgo.

parole.significato: family; nuclear family (a father, mother and their sons and daughters)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin familia (“household, family”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fantasia, from Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía).

Learned borrowing from Latin phantasma (“apparition, specter”), from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “an appearance, image, apparition, specter”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to make visible”). Doublet of abantesma.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fantastico, a learned borrowing from Latin phantasticus, borrowed from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós), from φαντάζω (phantázō) + -τικός (-tikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin fānāticus.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese faraó, faraón, from Late Latin Pharaōnem, from Ancient Greek Φαραώ (Pharaṓ), from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (par‘ōh), from Egyptian pr:aA (pr-ꜥꜣ, “palace, pharaoh”), from pr (“house”) + ꜥꜣ (“big”).
From Vulgar Latin *farellum, from Latin far (“spelt”). Cognate with Galician farelo and Asturian fariellu.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharyngem, borrowed from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx, “throat, gullet”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHg-, *bʰerH-, or Pre-Greek *?.
Learned borrowing from New Latin pharynx.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese farinha, from Latin farīna (“flour”), from far (“emmer”). Compare Galician, Fala, and Asturian fariña and Spanish harina.

parole.significato: a cabinet where medicine is stored
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “a drug, charm, enchantment”).

parole.significato: food made from manioc flour cooked in fat
parole.testo: Uncertain. * Possibly an African borrowing; see Kimbundu falofa, referencing a meal made with flour, oil, water, and peanuts. However some sources argue that the Kimbundu term may have been borrowed from Portuguese instead. * Perhaps from Latin far (“a type of hulled wheat”) + offa (“chunk; dumpling
From Old Galician-Portuguese farto, from Latin fartus. Cognate with Galician farto and Spanish harto. Doublet of harto
Borrowed from Latin fascināre.
Learned borrowing from Latin fasciculus.
Borrowed from Latin fasciola.
Learned borrowing from Latin fastīdiōsus. Doublet of fastioso.
Inherited from Latin fastīdium.
Borrowed from Latin fātālis (“fatal”).
Ultimately from Latin fatuus (“foolish”).

Learned borrowing from Latin factor (“a doer, maker, performer”), from factus (“done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). Doublet of feitor. Piecewise doublet of fazedor.

Borrowed from New Latin factoriālis, from Latin factor (“a doer, maker, performer”), from factus (“done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”).
Learned borrowing from Latin factūra. Doublet of feitura, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin fātidicus.

parole.significato: fauna (set of animal species that characterize a region or period)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fauna.

parole.significato: faun (country deity among the Romans, represented with goat's feet and horns)
parole.testo: From Latin faunus.
From Latin faustus.
From Latin fastus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fava, from Latin faba (“bean”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”).

parole.significato: a tree of species Cnidoscolus quercifolius, native to northeastern Brazil
parole.testo: The slum sense is named after the tree. The first favela was founded by veterans of the War of Canudos on Morro da Providência (Providence Hill). That hill was similar to a hill where a battle took place during the war, which had many favela trees. The name of the tree probably comes ultimately from
From Old Galician-Portuguese favo, from Latin favus, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw- (“to swell, grow, thrive, be, live, dwell”).
From Latin favor (“favour; good will”), from faveō (“to favour”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰoweh₁ (“to notice”).
Learned borrowing from Latin favōrābilis.

parole.significato: farm (a place where agricultural activities take place)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese fazenda, from Latin facienda, form of faciendus (“which is to do”), from faciō (“do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). Cognate with Spanish hacienda. Doublet of faina.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fazer. Compare Galician facer, Spanish hacer, Italian fare.
From Latin Phoebeus, related to Phoebus, the "radiant one", epithet of Apollo, the Greco-Roman god of the Sun, light, and the arts.
From Latin Phoebus, the "radiant one", epithet of Apollo, the Greco-Roman god of the Sun, light, and the arts.

parole.significato: fever (high body temperature due to disease)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese febre, fever, from Latin febris (“fever”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷhris or *bʰebʰris.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrilis, from Latin febris. By surface analysis, febre + -il.
Learned borrowing from Latin febrīcula (“light fever”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fechar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin pesclum, from Latin pessulus (“bolt”). Probably a southern Portuguese variant, with the change of /p/ to /f/ reflecting Arabic influence. By surface analysis, fecho + -ar.
Borrowed from Latin fecundus.
From Vulgar Latin *foeticosus, from foetidus.

parole.significato: to stink (have a strong bad smell)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese feder, from Latin fētēre, probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂-. Compare Spanish heder.

parole.significato: federal, federative (of or relating to a federation, a form of government that divides a sovereign state into smaller,…
parole.testo: Derived from Latin foedus. The slang sense comes from homem federal.
Learned borrowing from Latin foederātiōnem. By surface analysis, federar + -ção.

parole.significato: stench (a strong foul smell, a stink)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese fedor, from Latin fētōrem.

From Old Galician-Portuguese *feijõo, variant of feijoo, from Latin phaseolus, probably from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos). Doublet of Feijó. Cognate with Galician feixón, Ladino fijon, Spanish frijol, Catalan fesol and Italian fagiolo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese feo (“ugly”), from Latin foedus (“hideous”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂- (“to frighten; be afraid”). Cognate with Galician feo, Asturian feu and Spanish feo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese feira, from Late Latin feria (“festival, holiday”), from Latin feriae, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“god, godhead, deity”). Cognate with Galician feira, Spanish feria, French foire, Italian fiera, Sicilian fera and English fair. Doublet of féria
Inherited from Latin factīcius (“artificial”). Compare the borrowed doublets factício and fetiche. Cognate with Spanish hechizo. Related to feito (“done; deed”) and fato (“fact”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese feito, from Latin factum. Doublet of facto/fato.
From Latin factōrem. Doublet of fator. Piecewise doublet of fazedor.
From feitor + -ia, the stem from Latin factor, cognate with English factor.

From Old Galician-Portuguese feixe, from Latin fascis, from fascio (“to bundle”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰasko (“bundle, band”). Cognate with Galician feixe, Spanish haz, Catalan feix, Occitan fais, French faix, Italian fascio and Romanian fascie.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese feiçon, faiçon, from Latin factiōnem. Doublet of fa(c)ção, a learned borrowing, and fashion, from English.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fel, from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.

parole.significato: fellatio (stimulation of the penis with the mouth)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fellātiō, from fellō + -tiō.

parole.significato: happiness (state of someone who is happy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fēlīcitātem. Cognate with Galician felicidade.
Borrowed from Late Latin fēlīcitāre.
Borrowed from Latin fēlīnus (“feline”), from fēlēs (“cat”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese feliz, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin fēlīcem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-lw-i, from *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle”). The Old Galician-Portuguese form fiiz, however, was popularly inherited, but later replaced by feliz, in a process of restoration.

parole.significato: down (protruding hair from upholstery or fabric)
parole.testo: From Late Latin faluppa, through Old French felpe, perhaps ultimately of Germanic origin and borrowed from Frankish *felt. Compare Italian and Spanish felpa, and Sicilian ferpa.
From Latin fēmina (“woman”) + -al.
From Latin fēmina (“woman”) + -il.
Borrowed from Latin fēminīnus.
Inherited from Latin fēmineus (“womanly”).
From Latin findere, from Proto-Italic *findō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).
Borrowed from Latin fenestra. Compare the inherited doublet fresta.

Ultimately from Latin fēnum, monophthongized variant of faenum, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-. Judging by the unexpected retention of /-n-/ (compare Old Portuguese fẽo), possibly borrowed from or influenced by Asturian fenu. The motive could have been to avoid homophony with feo (“ugly”), a

Learned borrowing from Latin Phoenīcius (“phoenician”), from Phoenīcia (“Phoenicia”), from Ancient Greek Φοινίκη (Phoiníkē), from φοίνικι (phoíniki, “Phoenicians”), from Mycenaean Greek 𐀡𐀛𐀑𐀍 (po-ni-ki-jo), from Egyptian fnḫw (fenekhu, “Canaanites, Syrians”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phaenomenon, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”).
From Latin fera, from ferus.
From Latin ferāx.

parole.significato: holiday (day declared free from work by the state or government)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese feriado, from féria + -ado, from Latin fēria (“holiday”), from Proto-Indo-European *dhēs- (“god, godhead, deity”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese ferida, from Latin ferīta, from ferītus (“struck”), from feriō (“to stike”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to pierce, strike”). Compare Italian ferita, Spanish herida.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ferido, from Vulgar Latin *ferītus (“stricken”), perfect passive participle of feriō (“to strike”).

parole.significato: beastly (behaving like a beast; cruel or savage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferīnus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ferir, from Latin ferīre.
Borrowed from Latin fermentāre.
Learned borrowing from Latin fermentātiōnem. By surface analysis, fermentar + -ção.
Borrowed from Latin fermentum (“yeast”), from ferveō (“to boil”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ferōcitātem. By surface analysis, feroz + -idade.

parole.significato: fierce (extremely violent, severe, ferocious or savage)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ferox (“wild, untamed”).

parole.significato: tool (mechanical device intended to make a task easier)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin ferrāmenta, from the plural of Latin ferrāmentum.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ferreiro (compare Galician ferreiro), from Latin ferrārius (“blacksmith”) (compare Spanish herrero), from ferrum (“iron”). By surface analysis, ferro + -eiro.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ferro, from Latin ferrum, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: bolt (sliding pin or bar in a lock)
parole.testo: From a modification of Old Galician-Portuguese verrolho (influenced by ferro (“iron”)), from Vulgar Latin *verruculum, from Latin vericulum, diminutive of verū (“dart”). Compare development of Spanish cerrojo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ferrugen, from Latin ferrūginem.
Borrowed from Latin fertilitātem.
Inherited from Latin ferventem.

parole.significato: to boil (heat a liquid until it begins to turn into a gas)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ferver, from Latin fervēre, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeru- (“to be hot, boil”).
Borrowed from Latin fervōrem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese festa, from Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *festizāre. Derivable from festa + -ejar.

parole.significato: festive (having the atmosphere, decoration, or attitude of a festival or party)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fēstīvus.

parole.significato: fetus (human embryo after the eighth week of gestation)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fētus (“offspring”).

parole.significato: fern (any of a group of plants in the division Pteridophyta)
parole.testo: From earlier fento, from Old Galician-Portuguese *feeyto, from Latin filictum (“place abounding in ferns”), from filix, filicem (“fern”). Cognate with Galician fento, fieito and Spanish helecho.
Borrowed from Latin feudum.

From Old Galician-Portuguese fevereiro, fevreyro, febreyro, from Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin Februārius, from fēbruum (“purification”), via the purification ritual Fēbrua held on February 15 in the old Roman calendar.
From Latin faecem (“dregs”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fiar, from Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere. Compare Galician and Spanish fiar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fiar, from Late Latin fīlāre, from Latin fīlum. Derivable from fio + -ar. Compare Galician fiar, Spanish hilar.

parole.significato: fiber / fibre (single elongated piece of material)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fibra. Compare the inherited doublet fêvera.

parole.significato: to become; to get; to end up
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ficar (also fincar), from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”). Doublet of fincar.
Borrowed from Latin fictītius.
Learned borrowing from Latin fictiōnem.
From Latin fides dignus (literally “worthy of faith”).
From Latin fīdūciārius (“held in trust”), from fīdūcia (“trust”). By surface analysis, fidúcia + -ário.
From Latin fīdūcia (“trust”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese fiel, from Latin fidēlis.
From Old Galician-Portuguese figo, from Latin fīcus (“fig tree, fig (fruit)”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese figueira, from Latin fīcāria. By surface analysis, figo + -eira.
From Old Galician-Portuguese figura, fegura, borrowed from Latin figūra.
From Latin figūrātus, perfect passive participle of figūrō.

parole.significato: to look like; to resemble (be similar in appearance to)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin figūrāre (“to form”).
Borrowed from Late Latin figūrātīvus.
Borrowed from Latin figūrātiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin fīlāmentum, from Late Latin fīlō (“to spin, draw out in a long line”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

parole.significato: philanthropy (benevolent altruism with the intention of increasing the well-being of mankind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese filha (“daughter”), from Latin fīlia (“daughter”), from fīlius (“son”). Compare Galician filla.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese filho (“son”), from Latin fīlius (“son”), from Old Latin fīlios (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Compare Galician fillo, Spanish hijo and Sicilian figghiu.

parole.significato: a traditional christmas treat prepared with eggs and flour, fried in olive oil; beignet, fritter
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese folloa, from Vulgar Latin *foliola, diminutive of Latin folium. Compare Galician filloa, Spanish hojuela.

parole.significato: filial (pertaining to a son or daughter)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fīliālis.

parole.significato: phylum (rank below kingdom and above class)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin phylum.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese philosophia, from Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía), from φίλος (phílos, “beloved”) + σοφία (sophía, “wisdom”).
From Vulgar Latin *filōlum, diminutive of Latin filum.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese filósofo, from Latin philosophus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fim, fin, from Latin finis, of disputed origin. Perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- or Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd-.
Borrowed from Late Latin fīnālis, from fīnis. By surface analysis, fim + -al.

From Old Galician-Portuguese fincar, from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”). Doublet of ficar. The -n- may be due to the influence of Latin fingere and its derivatives.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fĩidar, from Vulgar Latin *fīnītāre, from Latin fīnītus, perfect passive participle of fīnīō.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *fĩido, from Latin fīnītus. Doublet of finito.

parole.significato: to pretend (to act as though something is different from what it is)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fingir, from Latin fingere.
Borrowed from Latin fīnītus (“finite; limited”), present passive participle of fīniō (“to finish; to limit”). Doublet of findo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fin, from Latin finis (“end”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰnh₂-.

parole.significato: Finnish (of or relating to Finland or Finns)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Finnus, from Proto-Germanic *finnaz.
From Latin fincta, variant of Latin ficta (“fake, fictitious”)
From Latin finita (“finished, finite”)

parole.significato: logistic (relating to the transportation of goods or supplies)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin logisticus, from Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós).
From Old Galician-Portuguese lombo, from Latin lumbus (“loin”), from Proto-Germanic *landwīn, *landwiō (“waist, loins”), from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰw- (“kidney, waist”).

parole.significato: giant roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides, a parasitic roundworm)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese lombriga, from Latin lumbricus, with a shift in gender.
From Old Galician-Portuguese longe, from Latin longe.
Learned borrowing from Latin longaevitātem.
Borrowed from Latin longaevus.

parole.significato: angular distance measured west or east of the Greenwich Meridian
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin longitūdō (“length, a measured length”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese longo, from Latin longus, from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós (“long”).
Learned borrowing from Latin longinquus (“far; remote”), from longus (“far, long”), from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós (“long”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese *lontra, from a Vulgar Latin variant of Latin lutra. First attested in Gil Vicente's Auto das Fadas. Cf. also Old Galician-Portuguese luntria, attested in 1253.
Borrowed from Latin loquācitātem.
Learned borrowing from Latin loquācem (“talkative”).
Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

parole.significato: bay (Laurus nobilis, a shrub of the Mediterranean)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese loureiro, from Vulgar Latin *laurārius, from Latin laurus. By surface analysis, louro (“laurel, laurel leaf”) + -eiro.
From Old Galician-Portuguese louro, from Latin laurus (“laurel”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese louvar, from earlier louar, loar, from Latin laudāre (“to praise”), from laus (“praise”). Piecewise doublet of laudar.

parole.significato: praise; worship (especially of a religious entity)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese louvor, loor, corresponding to louvar (“to praise”) + -or (“forms nouns indicating condition”), from Latin laudō (“to praise”), from laus (“praise, glory”).
From Latin lautia (“magnificence, splendor”), from lautus (“luxurious, washed”), or alternatively from lutea, luteus (“of clay”). Compare Galician louza, Spanish loza.

parole.significato: lotion (ointment to be rubbed on the skin)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lotiōnem, from lavō.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lũa, from Latin lūna (“moon”), from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, which is derived from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-. Cognate with Galician lúa, Spanish, Italian, and Occitan luna, Catalan lluna, French lune, an

From Latin luna nova (“new moon”). Compare Galician lúa nova, Spanish luna nueva, Catalan lluna nova, Occitan luna novèla, French nouvelle lune, Italian luna nuova and Romanian lună nouă.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lũar, from Latin lūnāris, from lūna (“moon”) + -āris. Doublet of lunar. Compare Galician luar.
Borrowed from Latin lucrārī. Compare the inherited lograr.
Learned borrowing from Latin lucrativus.
Borrowed from Latin lucrum. Doublet of logro (“fraud”), which was inherited..
From Latin ludus + -ismo.
From Latin lūdus (“play”) + pedem (“foot”) + -io. The coinage is sometimes attributed to Antônio de Castro Lopes, but the first attestation dates from 1921, 20 years after his death.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese logar, from Late Latin locālem (“local”), from Latin locus (“place”), from Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put”). Compare Galician lugar, Fala lugal, Asturian llugar, and Spanish lugar. Doublet of local.
From Latin lōlīgō (“squid, cuttlefish”).

parole.significato: flame, fire (to cook or keep oneself warm)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lume, from Latin lūmen. Cognate with Galician, French, Italian, and Romanian lume, Spanish lumbre, Catalan llum and Occitan lum. In the sense of "lumen" it is a modern neologism. Doublet of lúmen, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin lūminōsus. Compare the archaic inherited doublet lumioso.
Borrowed from Late Latin lūmināria, neuter plural of lūmināre, from Latin lūmen.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūnāris. Doublet of luar.
From Medieval Latin lūnātiō.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūnāticus.
Learned borrowing from Latin lupānārem.
Learned borrowing from Latin luscus (“one-eyed”).

parole.significato: Lusitanian (member of ancient Lusitania or its people)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lūsītānus.

parole.significato: Lusitanian (of or pertaining to ancient Roman province of Lusitania, its people or culture)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Lūsus (“Lusus, supposed Roman god”), from lūsus (“a play(ing), a game”).
From Lusitânia (“poetic name for Portugal”), from Latin Lūsitānia (“province of Roman Hispania”); and from luso (“Portuguese”), from Luso (“Lusus, supposed Roman god”), from Latin lūsum (“game”).
Borrowed from Latin lūstrum, denoting a lavatory sacrifice after a quinquennial census, possibly cognate to luō (“to wash, to cleanse”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese luita, from Late Latin lucta, from Latin luctor. Compare Galician loita and Spanish lucha.
From earlier luitador, from Latin lūctātōrem (compare Spanish luchador). By surface analysis, lutar + -dor.
From Old Galician-Portuguese luitar, from Latin luctārī. Compare Galician loitar, Spanish luchar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese luito, from Latin lūctus (“grief, sorrow”). Compare Galician loito.
Borrowed from Latin lux. Doublet of the inherited luz.
From Latin luxāre. By surface analysis, luxo (“luxury”) + -ar

parole.significato: dislocation; luxation (dislocating of an organ from its proper place, especially a bone from a joint)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin luxātiōnem. By surface analysis, luxar + -ção
From Latin luxus (“extravagance, luxury”).
Learned borrowing from Latin lūxuriōsus.

parole.significato: lust (strong desire, especially of a sexual nature)
parole.testo: From Latin luxuria.

parole.significato: light (medium within which vision is possible)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese luz, from Latin lūcem, from Proto-Italic *louks, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- (“white; light; bright”). Doublet of lux. Compare Galician luz.
From Old Galician-Portuguese luzerna, from Latin lucerna.
From Old Galician-Portuguese luzir, from Vulgar Latin *lūcīre from Latin lūcēre.

parole.significato: there (in that place, far from both the speaker and the audience)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ala, from Latin ad (“to”) + illāc (“that way”).
From Latin labium (“lip”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”).

parole.significato: dairy (relating to milk-based products or processes)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lacteus, from lac (“milk”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese lagrima, lagrema, from Latin lacrima, from Old Latin lacruma, dacrima, dacruma, from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru-, from earlier compound *dr̥ḱ-h₂eḱru- (“eye bitter”).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Latin lepore.
Borrowed from Latin lapidem (“stone”). Doublet of lápis.

parole.significato: latex (milky sap used to make rubber)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin latex (“clear fluid which is part of a humour or bodily fluid”), a later use of Latin latex (“water; liquid, fluid”).
Borrowed from Latin laureus.
Borrowed from Latin laureus.
Learned borrowing from Latin lāmina.

From Old Galician-Portuguese lampada, borrowed from Late Latin lampada, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “lamp or flambeau”), from Ancient Greek λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”). Compare the inherited Old Portuguese form lampaa.

parole.significato: languid; listless (lacking enthusiasm, energy or strength)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin languidus.

parole.significato: wool (wavy fur of sheep and other animals)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lãa, from Latin lāna. Cognate with Catalan llana, French laine, Galician laa, Italian lana, Occitan lana, Romanian lână and Spanish lana.

parole.significato: legua, Portuguese league, a traditional unit of distance, variously reckoned as 4444.4, 5555.6, or 6172.8 m
parole.testo: From Late Latin leuga (“Gaulish league, the distance of one hour's walking”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *lougā. Cognate with Spanish and Galician legua and Catalan llegua.
Learned borrowing from Latin lepidus.

parole.significato: lemures (spirits or ghosts of the dead)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lemures (“the ghosts of the dead”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese *lendẽa, from Late Latin lendina, ultimately from Latin lendem. Compare Galician lendia.
From Old Galician-Portuguese levedo, from Vulgar Latin *levĭtum (“yeast, sourdough”), from Latin levātus (“lifted”). Compare Galician lévedo, Spanish leudo.
Borrowed from Latin liber (“inner bark”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Lycius.
Learned borrowing from Latin licitus (“lawful”).

Borrowed from Latin limpidus. Compare limpo, an inherited doublet.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lingua (“tongue, language”), from Latin lingua.
Borrowed from Latin līchēn, from Ancient Greek λειχήν (leikhḗn), from λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”).
Learned borrowing from Latin liquidus (“fluid, liquid, moist”), from liqueō (“to be liquid, to be fluid”).
Learned borrowing from Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós), from λύρα (lúra, “lyre”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese liro, lílio, from Latin līlium, from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion). Doublet of lis.
Learned borrowing from New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λῐ́θος (lĭ́thos, “stone”) + -ium.
From Latin līvidus.
Learned borrowing from Latin locus. Doublet of logo.
Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

From Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”), from the feminine form of λογικός (logikós, “of or relating to speech or reason or reasoning, rational, reasonable”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, reason”).

parole.significato: logical (in agreement with the principles of logic)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin logicus.

parole.significato: lotus (an aquatic flowering plant of the genus Nelumbo)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

parole.significato: pike (any fish of the genus Esox)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lūcius.
Borrowed from Latin lugubris. Cf. also lôbrego.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūmen. Doublet of lume.

parole.significato: hop (plant whose flowers are used in ale brewing, Humulus lupulus)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lupulus. Compare Italian luppolo and Spanish lúpulo.

parole.significato: yellowish; yellow with a tinge or orange or red

Borrowed from Latin macedonicus.

Borrowed from Latin mācerātiōnem.

parole.significato: axe (tool and weapon consisting of a heavy blade on the end of a shaft)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese machado, from Latin marculātus, from marculus (“hammer”).

parole.significato: male (belonging or referring to the sex having the smaller gametes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese macho, from Vulgar Latin masclus. Doublet of másculo.
From the verb machar (“to grind”), from macho (“mallet”), from Latin marculus (“small hammer”). Compare Spanish machucar.
From maçã + -eira, from Old Galician-Portuguese maçẽeyra, from Medieval Latin mazanaria.
From Latin macilentus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese maciço, from Vulgar Latin *massīcius. By surface analysis, massa + -iço. Compare Spanish macizo. Doublet of massivo.

parole.significato: to taint (to contaminate or corrupt something with an external agent, either physically or morally)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin maculāre. Doublet of manchar and magoar.

parole.significato: wood (substance making up the central part of the trunk and branches of a tree)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese madeira, from Latin māteria, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr (“mother”). Doublet of matéria, a learned borrowing. Cognates include Galician madeira and Spanish madera.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin mataxa, from Ancient Greek μέταξα (métaxa).

parole.significato: stepmother (wife of one's biological father, not one's biological mother)
parole.testo: From Late Latin mātrastra (“stepmother”), from Latin māter (“mother”), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Compare Galician madrasta, Spanish madrastra.
From Old Galician-Portuguese madre, from Latin māter, mātrem (“mother, matron”), from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Doublet of mãe.

parole.significato: honeysuckle (any plant of the genus Lonicera)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin matrisilva. Cognate with Galician, Spanish, and Italian madreselva.
From Old Galician-Portuguese madrỹa, from Early Medieval Latin mātrīna, from Latin mater (“mother”). Compare Galician madriña.
From Old Galician-Portuguese madrugar, madurgar, from Vulgar Latin *mātūricāre, derived from Latin mātūrāre (“hurry”) (whence Portuguese madurar).

Borrowed from Latin magistrātus (“magistrate”).

parole.significato: teachership or professorship (the occupation of a teacher or professor, or the exercise thereof)

Borrowed from Latin magnanimitātem.
From Latin magnātum, magnātēs.
Borrowed from Latin magnificentia (“greatness”).

Learned borrowing from Latin magnanimus, from magnus (“great”) + animus (“soul, mind”).

parole.significato: magnetic (of, relating to, caused by, or operating by magnetism)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin magnēticus. By surface analysis, magnete + -ico.

parole.significato: magnificent (grand, elegant or splendid in appearance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin magnificus (“great in deeds or sentiment, noble, splendid”), derived from Latin magnus (“great”), from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“great”).
Borrowed from Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos), from Old Iranian.
From mágoa or taken from Latin maculāre. Doublet of manchar and macular.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese magro, from Latin macrum, from Proto-Italic *makros, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós, from *meh₂ḱ- + *-rós.

parole.significato: an Iberian festival, celebrated with roasted chestnuts and wine
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly partially from Latin ustus (“burned”). Cognate with Galician magosto, Asturian amagüestu and Spanish magosto.

From maior (“bigger; greater”) + -ia (“-y”), from Old Galician-Portuguese maior, from Latin maior (“bigger; greater”), from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“great”) + *-yos (“comparative suffix”).

parole.significato: used to form the comparative of adjectives and adverbs; more; -er
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mais, from Latin magis (“more”). Doublet of mas. Displaced collateral form chus.
Calque of Latin plūsquamperfectus. Literally, “more than perfect”.
Borrowed from Latin māiusculus.

parole.significato: majesty (the quality of being impressive and great)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese magestade, majestade, borrowed from Latin maiestātem.
Borrowed from Latin male (“badly”).
From Latin mala (“cheek”).
From Late Latin malitātem, from Latin malus. By surface analysis, mal + -dade. Compare Spanish maldad.

parole.significato: cursed, accursed, damned (inflicted with supernatural harm)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese maldito, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin maledictus.
From Latin maledīcere (“to slander, to curse”).
Possibly a semi-learned borrowing from Latin maledictiōnem (“curse, evil speech”).
Learned borrowing from Latin maleficium.
Inherited from Latin maledicta.
Borrowed from Latin malevolentem, from male (“badly, wrongly”) + volēns (“willing, wishing”), from volō (“to wish”).
Borrowed from Latin malevolentia.

parole.significato: to practice evil, to do evil things
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin malefacere. By surface analysis, mal- + fazer.

parole.significato: badly made; of low quality; crude; rough
parole.testo: mal + feito, or from Latin malefactus.
From Late Latin malefactōrem, from Latin malefaciō. Compare French malfaiteur, Spanish malhechor.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *madiga, from Latin magida, from Ancient Greek μαγίδα (magída).
From Old Galician-Portuguese mal(o) + grado, which stems from Latin grātum (see grātus (“pleasing, acceptable, agreeable, welcome”)). Compare Catalan malgrat and French malgré.
From Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“stain”). Compare the doublets mancha, malha, mácula, mágoa, and mangra.
From malhar (“to hammer; to beat”), from malho (“mallet; sledgehammer”), from Latin malleus (“hammer”).
Inherited from Latin malleus (“hammer; mallet”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
From older *malhe (“flail”), from Latin manualis (“manual”), influenced by Latin malleus (“hammer”). Cognate with mangual.

parole.significato: malicious (of, pertaining to, or as a result of malice or spite)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin malitiōsus.
From Latin malignitātem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese maligno, borrowed from Latin malignus (“malignant”).

parole.significato: typhoid fever (a deadly disease characterised by severe fever)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin maligna.

parole.significato: mallow (any plant of the family Malvaceae)
parole.testo: From Latin malva, of Semitic origin.
Borrowed from Latin maleficus, from male (“badly, evilly”) + facio (“do”).

parole.significato: malevolent (having or displaying ill will; wishing harm on others)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin malevolus.
Learned borrowing from Latin malitia. Doublet of maleza.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mamar, from Late Latin mammō, from Latin mamma (“breast”) + -ō. By surface analysis, mama + -ar.
From mamila, from Latin mamilla.
Learned borrowing from Latin mammiferum, from mamma (“teat”) + ferō (“to bear”). By surface analysis, mamar (“to suckle”) + -ífero.

parole.significato: herd (number of domestic animals assembled together)
parole.testo: From Latin manuāta, from manus (“hand”).

parole.significato: to ooze (be secreted or slowly leak)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mānāre (“pour or gush forth”).
From Vulgar Latin *mancipius (“slave”), from Latin mancipium (“purchase property”), also "a bought slave". For sense "coatrack" compare English valet.

parole.significato: stain, blemish, mark, spot (discoloured spot or visible impression)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *macla (probably through a variant with a nasal infix *mancla), from Latin macula (“stain, spot”). Doublet of the borrowed terms mácula, malha, mágoa, mangra, and maquis.
From Vulgar Latin *manclāre, *maclāre, from Latin maculāre. Doublet of magoar and macular.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese manco, from Latin mancus (“maimed”), from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂n-ko- (“maimed in the hand”), from *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én- (“hand”).
Borrowed from Latin mancipium (“right to property”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese mandar, from Latin mandāre (“to order, to commission”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mandātum. Piecewise doublet of mandado.
Learned borrowing from Latin mandragora.
Learned borrowing from Latin mandibula (“mandible”), from mandō (“to bite; to chew”).

parole.significato: manner; way (particular method of doing something)

Borrowed from Latin manes.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese manga, from Latin manica, from manus or -ica. Cognate with Spanish manga, French manche. Doublet of Mancha.

parole.significato: handle (part of an object which is held in the hand)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mango, from Early Medieval Latin manicus, from Latin manus (“hand”).

parole.significato: mildew (growth of minute fungi on plants)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“blemish”), probably via Spanish mangla. Doublet of mancha, malha, mágoa, mácula, and maquis.

parole.significato: act (a display of behaviour meant to deceive)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese manna, from Vulgar Latin *mania (“manual skill”), from Latin manus (“hand”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish maña.

From Old Galician-Portuguese mannãa (“morning”), from Vulgar Latin *maneāna (“morning”), from Latin māne (“in the morning”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, to mature”). Cognate with Galician mañá, Asturian mañana, Leonese mañana, Mirandese manhana, Spanish mañana, and Aragonese manyana.

Learned borrowing from Latin manifestātiōnem. By surface analysis, manifestar + -ção.

parole.significato: marjoram (Origanum majorana, a herb of the mint family)

From Vulgar Latin *mānsus, from Latin mānsuetus.
Borrowed from Latin mānsiōnem. Compare Spanish mansión. See also the doublet mesão, borrowed through Old French.

parole.significato: cloak (long outer garment worn over the shoulders covering the back)
parole.testo: From Late Latin mantum.
Learned borrowing from Latin manuālis.

Formed from Latin manu (“hand”) + -s- + -ear.
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). See mania.

Borrowed from Latin māchinālis.

parole.significato: to engineer (to plan or achieve a goal by contrivance or guile)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin māchinārī (“scheme, plot”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: machination (clever scheme or artful plot, usually crafted for evil purposes)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin māchinātiōnem.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mar (“sea”), from Latin mare (“sea”), from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri. Compare Galician mar.

parole.significato: wonder; marvel (something that causes amazement or awe)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese maravilha, from Latin mīrābilia, plural of mīrābilis (“wonderful”), from mīrus (“wonderful”).

parole.significato: mixed (having two or more separate aspects)

parole.significato: mixture, blend (various different things put together)

parole.significato: misery, distress (extreme pain of body or mind)

parole.significato: modern (pertaining to the current time and style)

parole.significato: modest; humble (not bragging or boasting about oneself)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin modestus.

parole.significato: mode; way; method (method or manner of doing something)

Learned borrowing from Latin mōlēs. Doublet of mó, an inheritance.

parole.significato: to trouble; to bother; to annoy; to harass
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin molestāre (“to bother”), from molestus (“troublesome”).

parole.significato: softness; flabbiness; floppiness; flaccidity (the condition of being soft, flabby; lack of firmness)
parole.testo: From mole (“flaccid”) + -eza, perhaps corresponding to Latin mollitia, which would make it a doublet of molícia, sometimes used as a synonym. Compare Spanish molleza, Italian mollezza.

parole.significato: covered with or impregnated with liquid; wet
parole.testo: Past participle of molhar, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre, from Latin mollīre. Compare Spanish mojado, Galician mollado, Catalan mullat, Occitan molhat, French mouillé.
From Old Galician-Portuguese mollar, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“soak”), a verb based on Latin mollis (“soft”). Compare Galician mollar, Spanish mojar.
Deverbal from molhar (“to wet; to water”), from Old Galician-Portuguese mollar, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“to soak”), from Latin mollis (“soft”), from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dus (“soft, weak”).

parole.significato: bundle (group of objects held together by wrapping or tying, especially keys or vegetables)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mãollo, from Late Latin manuc(u)lus, modified ultimately from manipulus (“maniple; handful”), from manus (“hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *man-. Doublet of manolho and manojo. Compare Spanish manojo.

Learned borrowing from Latin mollitia (“softness, pliability”). Doublet of moleza, of which it is a synonym in some contexts.

Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).

parole.significato: monarchy (form of government with a hereditary head of state)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía). By surface analysis, mono- + -arquia.
Learned borrowing from Latin monastērium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion). Doublet of mosteiro.

Learned borrowing from Latin monētārius. Piecewise doublet of moedeiro.
Learned borrowing from Latin monitōrem.

parole.significato: monogamy (form of relationship in which an individual has only one partner during their lifetime or at any one time)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin monogamia, from Ancient Greek μονογαμία (monogamía). By surface analysis, mono- + -gamia.
Learned borrowing from Latin monopolĭum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monosyllabicus, from Latin monosyllabus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μονοσύλλαβος (monosúllabos). By surface analysis, mono- + silábico.
Borrowed from Latin mōnstrum.
From Old Galician-Portuguese montanna, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.
From Late Latin montāniōsus, an adjective based on montānia, from Latin montem (“mountain”). By surface analysis, montanha + -oso.

parole.significato: mountain (relating to a mountain or mountainous region)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin montānus.

parole.significato: mount; a mountain or large hill
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese monte m, from Latin montem m. Compare Galician monte m.
Borrowed from Late Latin monumentālis.

parole.significato: monument (a structure built for commemorative or symbolic reasons)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese monumento, borrowed from Latin monumentum. Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese mõimento.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monasticus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monotonus, from Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos).

Learned borrowing from Latin mora (“delay”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese morador, from Latin morātōrem.
Learned borrowing from Latin mōrālis.

parole.significato: morality (recognition of or obedience to the rules of correct conduct)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mōrālitātem.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese morar, probably borrowed from Latin morārī.

parole.significato: moratorium (authorization permitting temporary suspension of payments)
parole.testo: Feminine of moratório (“moratory”), from Late Latin morātōrium, neuter substantival use of Latin morātōrius (“delaying”), from moror (“to delay”), from mora (“delay”).
Learned borrowing from Latin morbus, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *mer-. Doublet of mormo.

parole.significato: bat (any flying mammal of the order Chiroptera)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese murcego, from Vulgar Latin *mūrem caecus, by surface analysis, mure (“mouse”) + cego (“blind”). Compare Galician morcego, Spanish murciélago.

parole.significato: blood sausage, pudding (sausage made primarily from blood)
parole.testo: Uncertain, possibly from Latin [Term?]. See Spanish morcela, Spanish morcilla.

parole.significato: mordacious (sharp or caustic in style or tone)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mordācem (“biting”).

parole.significato: gag (object placed in someone’s mouth to prevent them from speaking and biting)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mordacia, from Latin mordāx, mordācia (“biting”). Compare Spanish mordaza and Italian mordacchia.
From Old Galician-Portuguese morder, from Latin mordēre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese moordomo, mayordomo, from Late Latin maior domūs (“steward”), from Latin maior (“main, principal”) + genitive singular of domus (“household”).

parole.significato: moray (any eel of the family Muraenidae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *morẽa, from Latin murēna, from Ancient Greek μῡ́ραινα (mū́raina). Cognate with Galician morea.

parole.significato: morganatic (between a man of higher rank and a woman of lower rank)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morganāticus, from Late Latin mātrimōnium ad morganāticam, from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō (“morning-gift”), from *murginaz (“morning”) + *gēbǭ (“gift”).
Learned borrowing from Latin moribundus (“dying”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *murrum (“muzzle, snout”).

parole.significato: mortality (the condition of being susceptible to death)

parole.significato: mortar (small vessel used to grind things)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mortārium (“mortar”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mortificāre.

Learned borrowing from Latin mortiferum, derived from mors (“death”) + -fer (“-bearing, -carrying”), originally a calque of Ancient Greek θᾰνᾰτηφόρος (thănătēphóros, “deadly, lethal”, literally “death-bearing”). By surface analysis, morte + -ífero.

parole.significato: fly (various insects in the order Diptera)

From Old Galician-Portuguese mosto, from Latin mustum, neuter of mustus (“fresh, young", and, of wine, "unfermented”), from Proto-Indo-European *mus-, *mews- (“damp”).

Borrowed from Latin mōtus.

From Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).

parole.significato: metric (of or relating to the metric system)

parole.significato: narcissus; daffodil (any of several bulbous flowering plants of the genus Narcissus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).

parole.significato: offer (a proposal that has been made)

parole.significato: offertory (part of the mass in which the priest offers the host and chalice)
parole.testo: From Late Latin offertorium, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Catalan and Spanish ofertorio, Italian offertorio.

From Old Galician-Portuguese oitavo, from Latin octāvus. Cognate with Galician oitavo, Spanish ochavo, and Catalan octau.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarquia (“oligarchy”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: omasum (the third part of the stomach of a ruminant)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin omāsum.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ombro, from Latin umerus (“shoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”). Doublet of úmero.

parole.significato: who hasn't foreseen, included or mentioned a particular possibility/circumstance.

Borrowed from Late Latin omissiōnem, from Latin omittō.

parole.significato: to omit (to leave out or exclude)

parole.significato: omnivore (animal which eats both plants and meat)

From Old Galician-Portuguese onda, from Latin unda (“wave”).

parole.significato: where; wherever (in or at what place; in or at a/any/the place that, in what situation)

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese onze, from Latin ūndecim.

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese onça, from Latin ū̆ncia (“unit, ¹⁄₁₂ pound”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”). As an English unit, a semantic loan of English ounce. Cognate with Galician and Spanish onza, Catalan unça, French once, and English ounce and inch.
Borrowed from Latin opācitātem.

parole.significato: opaque (allowing little light to pass through)

parole.significato: operation (method by which a device performs its function)
